en: The Monastic Rules for Huanzhu Hermitage, by National Teacher Puying (with Preface). The *Analects* state:
"When the gentleman studies the Way, he loves others; when the commoner studies the Way, he is easy to direct. Master Zhuang [said]:...
It is also said: "Fish forget one another in rivers and lakes; people forget one another in the Way and its arts.

If even the way of entering the world can thus be easily practiced so that they forget each other, how much more so the way of Buddhas and Patriarchs appearing in the world, which blends self and other and equalizes oneself and others—wherein all things interpenetrate and merge without any interval?
When the mind dwells in the Way, it naturally accords with the Mean without depending on ritual forms. Not...
If one waits for the Dharma, one will naturally become upright; what need is there then to speak of the rules and regulations of the monastic groves (*saṃghārāma*)?
Alas, it has been long since the human heart has strayed from the Way. More than fifteen hundred years ago, it had already fallen into disintegration.

Baizhang arose and established the monastic groves to rescue it; yet even now, they cannot be free of defects. At this present hermitage, we certainly do not dare to emulate the formal protocols of the monastic groves.
Furthermore, as daily practice must not violate established norms or disrupt the fundamental principles, I have composed this brief work titled *The Essential Knowledge*, arranged into ten sections.
It serves as a standard for the mutual interpenetration of the primary and its attendants and establishes the regulations for a distinct school; it is not intended to compete with the Great Dharma.

Should there be practitioners who engage in genuine inquiry and earnest investigation, they should collect their thoughts during moments when the innate nature has not yet dispersed, throughout the entire day.

One acts without perceiving the toil; one rests all day without knowing the ease. When one forgets ritual and law externally and empties the subject-object duality internally, such a compilation is like a superfluous growth;
how then could I dare decline it? Written in the winter of the Ding-si year of the Yan-you era by the monk Huanzhu.
Ten Essential Items for Daily Life:
Daily Sustenance, Monthly Progression, Annual Regulations, Worldly Models, Household Management, Social Roles,
Conduct, Nourishment, Funerary Rites, and Escorting the Deceased.
In the teachings of the Japanese tradition, it is said that there are the first watch of the day, the middle watch of the day, and the last watch of the day;

furthermore, there are the first part of the night, the middle part of the night, and the latter part of the night—this is what the ancient masters referred to as "three periods of the day and three periods of the night. It is further stated: "When the daylight is insufficient, one should continue with..."
At night. Those who follow the Way by nature must not waste even a moment’s time, remaining inseparable from it for even an instant.

Throughout the six periods of day and night, how could there not be that which provides support? What is called "daily support" refers collectively to the standards observed during the twelve periods of the day and night.
The duties of a single hermitage take the discernment of the Way as their priority. The Way has no beginning or end; it arises in daily life.
As it is so one day, so it is every day. Only fearing that the day may not suffice, one continues it through the night; this is collectively termed the business of daily life.
Prepare a tray of incense, using three sticks as the standard measure. Begin burning them at dusk; by the time the third stick has burned, it will be approximately the fourth watch.
Meanwhile, boil noodle soup over the hearth. Three strikes of the wooden board are sounded in front of the hall.

The assembly withdraws their pillows and tucks back their quilts, folds their single-layered mats in half on their inner beds, descends to the floor to wash their faces, and returns to the hall to sit in meditation until the board signaling the end of the session is struck.

Upon the sounding [of the board], one immediately folds the bedding, dons the robe, and prostrates before the Buddha. Returning to the bowl-position, one sits and spreads out the bowl to receive the gruel. When the gruel is finished, one recites a scripture before the Buddha.
Upon completing the scripture, there is a brief rest. Before the hall, the board sounds three times again; from the master down to the attendants, they return to the hall to sit in meditation.
When it is time for the midday meal, the fire-board sounds and they descend to the ground. After a short while, the long board sounds, and they return to the bowl-position to receive [the food].

They eat. When the meal is finished, they rest briefly. Three strikes of the board sound before the hall, and they return to the hall to sit in meditation. At the hour of *bū* (late afternoon), the board sounds to signal the end of the session.
At dusk, the incense burner is lit; the assembly dons their robes, recites sutras, and performs the ritual of offering food, which concludes when it is finished.
When the wooden board sounds three times before the hall, the assembly returns to the hall to sit in meditation.

When the board for the end of the session (*fangcan*) sounds, they remove their pillows, unfold their blankets, and rest on their right sides. This is the standard daily routine for the great assembly;
its general meaning is largely the same as that found in the *Conglin Qinggui*, though this text merely extracts its essential points.
During the four periods of seated meditation within each day and night, one should respectively clear the mind and sever all discursive thoughts, stilling the mind and forgetting external conditions.

One must deeply investigate the nature of birth and death and exert oneself to the utmost in the practice of the Way. Except for the times of attending to the necessities of nature, no conversation is permitted.

Washing and laundering are not permitted; mending and patching are not permitted; reading and reciting are not permitted. Furthermore, no miscellaneous tasks whatsoever are allowed, except for those performed as part of the communal labor (*pǔqǐng*) of the monastic community.
Whether ascending to the bed or descending from it, leaving the hall or entering the room, one must act as if walking on thin ice or standing by a deep precipice.
Do not allow your fellow residents to become aware of your movements, lest they disturb their path. Thus, the mind will naturally assist the body internally and externally.
It is silent and still.

The moon advances day by day until it becomes a month; months accumulate to form a year. Worldly phenomena flow and shift, and all things, both self and other, undergo transformation together with time.
The seasonal periods also require one another to meet; since they are said to be established, how could they be left unregulated? Daily provisions are insufficient, so they are supplemented monthly.
This is not merely a plan to follow along with temporal conditions, but is intended so that everyone may know of it.
On the first day of the first month, the New Year’s Day, the bells and wooden clappers are struck at the fifth watch and the assembly gathers.

After the *Mahākaruṇā-mantra* has been recited for the blessing of the Emperor, the congregation offers congratulations in the same manner as during the four seasonal festivals. On this day, a vegetarian feast (*zhāi*) is prepared; at the midpoint of the meal, [the scriptures] are chanted.
The Universal Dedication of Merit of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra.
On the fifteenth day, the Lantern Festival of the Upper Prime (the first month), offerings are prepared as appropriate. Early on this day, at the full moon, one offers prayers for the Emperor.
However, throughout the twelve months of the year, whenever the first or fifteenth day occurs, these are called the New Moon and Full Moon; on such occasions, one must partake of congee.

Recite the Great Compassion Mantra before the gruel to offer prayers for the Sage; this cycle repeats once every year. Among these days, there are six that are one’s own birthday (birth-star day), which are auspicious days.
These six days are treated the same as the new and full moons. Recite the Great Compassion Mantra before the gruel on these days to offer prayers for the Sage.
I reflect deeply upon this:
The Imperial Grace is like the sky covering all. We, who are as frail as the ancient groves and springs, have received the Emperor’s bounty and attained lifelong peace.
How could the sincerity of our prayers and praises be restricted to specific days?
Indeed, throughout the twenty-four hours of the day—whether looking up, looking down, turning, or moving—it is always a time for giving thanks and offering prayers. Now, we specifically select...
That which is performed on one’s birth year and the new and full moons is intended to manifest [the sacred presence] outwardly; this preface is respectfully inscribed here.

No records are kept for other months. On the first, sixteenth, and twenty-sixth days of every month—the times when the assembly of all the sages convenes—the permanent monastery prepares incense, flowers, lamps, candles, tea, fruits, and delicacies, setting them out as offerings in the Hall of the Local Deity. Great...
The assembly shall recite the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī every month according to this rule.
At the end of each month, there shall be five or six lines on a blank sheet of paper for matters that must regularly be included, to be filled in as required.
On the third day of the second lunar month,
the ceremony for the auspicious occasion of the Emperor’s Birthday was inaugurated (the details are fully contained in the Annual Regulations and are not repeated here).
On the fifteenth day is the Buddha’s *parinirvāṇa*. On this day, one should prepare incense, candles, tea, fruit, delicacies, and all implements for offering.
One should also pre-compose a memorial inscription. At the time of the half-day meal, the wooden board shall be struck.

The assembly, each assuming their proper dignified demeanor, shall gather before the Buddha. The abbot comes forward to offer incense, then withdraws and performs three prostrations without folding his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), then advances once more.

When the serving of hot soup and the presentation of food before the incense burner are completed, withdraw and perform three prostrations. Again, light incense, present the monetary offering (*dakṣiṇā*), and finish serving the tea;
then, withdraw and again perform three prostrations. Fold up the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), approach the incense burner once more, and insert a single stick of incense.

Withdraw and, together with the assembly, perform three prostrations (in other monasteries, the two orders of officers step forward from the ranks to burn incense, but this may be waived for those residing in hermitages). Upon rising from the prostrations, the memorial text (*śāstra*) is then recited.

[The recitation] concluded. Then, he raised the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī and performed the dedication, saying: "By the extraordinary merit of this chanting, may it be dedicated to the true suchness of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
May it adorn the unsurpassed *bodhi* of the Buddha-fruit. May the four debts of gratitude be fully repaid and all beings in the three realms of existence be equally sustained.

May all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm together perfect the wisdom of all seeds. To all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, and all honored Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas..."
Sā. Mahāprajñāpāramitā. On the eighth day of the fourth lunar month is the Buddha’s birthday; on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month is the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment.

These two days are both identical to the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, though they will not be further discussed hereafter. Only on the eighth day of the fourth lunar month is there a widespread bathing of the Buddha.

The ritual procedures for this day are as follows: on the nineteenth day is the birthday of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. On this day, the offerings, the ceremonial protocols, and the proclamation of the *śāstra* (explanatory texts) are largely identical to those observed at the occasion of the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa;
however, the assembly does not perform formal lectures or prostrations. Nevertheless, one may still establish [the practice] according to individual capacity.
The ritual is established.
On the third day of the third month, the ceremony is concluded and dispersed.

The Ritual for the Holy Birthday (the necessary preparations are detailed in the Annual Regulations and are not repeated here; on this day, the offering of noodles is a universal custom throughout all quarters).
On the fourth day, the birthday of the Temple Guardian is celebrated; the permanent residents prepare offerings and chant sutras.
On the twenty-third day, the anniversary of the compassionate passing of Master Gaofeng was observed; at midday, an altar was established for offerings, and the assembly recited the Śūraṃgama-mantra.
The fourth month.
On the eighth day, the anniversary of the Buddha’s birth, a flower pavilion is prepared in advance to symbolize the newborn Buddha standing peacefully within a basin of scented water.
Two small ladles are provided, and while the abbot serves the meal, the assembly rises from their prostrations.
The Rector (Vina) recites the verse for bathing the Buddha, which the assembly joins in chanting. This begins with the abbot, the head seat, and the rest of the assembly.

Proceeding in order around until reaching the Buddha’s presence, one takes the ladle and scoops hot water to bathe the Buddha. When the rites for both the *saṃgha* and the *śramaṇas* are completed, one immediately recites the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī.

The offerings presented above, the proclamation of the memorial text (*sūtra*), and the subsequent dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) following the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī are all identical to those performed at the time of the *Nirvāṇa*;
they will not be detailed here again.
From the thirteenth day, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* assembly begins (the details are found in the *Niangui*).

On the evening of the fourteenth, during the evening recitation (*wanchan*), one must prepare incense, flowers, lamps, candles, tea, fruit, and delicacies to adorn the Land Deity Hall (*Tuditan*) according to the ritual rules.
The abbot burns incense and serves tea and soup; then, withdrawing, he stands in his assigned position. The *Weina*...
Then the recitation begins. When it is finished, the wooden board is struck in front of the hall, and the assembly returns to the hall.
In the storehouse, incense is burned and a full set of hot water is prepared before the Sacred Monk (Śākyamuni).
This same procedure applies to all four seasonal festivals.
The Fifteenth Day: Entering Retreat (details are provided in the *Niangui*).
Discourse on the Rituals for Host and Guest upon Entering Retreat. (The Host says:
"On this day of early summer, as we observe the proper season, we respectfully wish that the Master, the Seat-Holder and Elder of our community, may enjoy good health and well-being."

How great is my merit! That I, [Name], have long ago been blessed with the good fortune of being able to reside together with you—on this day when the imperial decree has arrived—I pray that you may rely upon the power of the Dharma for support.
I further hope that your spiritual conditions will be fully perfected. In presenting these humble congratulations, I am deeply ashamed of my lack of devotion.
My innermost feelings are filled with boundless joy and gratitude.
(The Guest said: "On this day of early summer, at the proper season, we respectfully wish that the Abbot, our venerable elder and teacher, may enjoy good health and receive every blessing.

This humble servant has had the great fortune over many lifetimes to find refuge under your guidance. On this auspicious occasion of the commencement of the retreat, we look up to you with hope that you will continue to bestow your compassion without weariness and grant us blessings at all times.
May you far uphold the scales of authority of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, forever acting as a guide for humans and devas."
This is the standard for such matters. My congratulations are not exclusive [to you alone]. I am filled with a sense of shame and gratitude beyond measure.
On the fifth day of the fifth month, the Duanwu Festival.
On the twenty-eighth day, the Three-Day Sūtra Assembly for the Green Sprouts shall commence; it will conclude on the first day of the sixth month.

One must prepare incense, candles, and ritual offerings, as well as draft the formal petition (*śāstra*) and issue the list of sūtras in advance, so that the assembly may gather to cultivate merit by reading them.
Thereafter, the titles of the sūtras shall be compiled into the petition for the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*).
The dispersal of the Green Sprout Assembly on the first day of the sixth month is also a custom of the midsummer season.
The seventh month...
On the thirteenth day, the *Lengyan* assembly concluded with the distribution of offerings.
On the evening of the fourteenth, there was chanting at the *Tandi* Hall during the evening service.

On the fifteenth, the formal conclusion of the retreat (*jie zhi*) and social greetings were performed. That night, the extraordinary *Yulanpen* assembly was inaugurated for the purpose of providing relief.
In this secluded and refreshing place, we shall repay their labors.

For this assembly, you must also prepare individual copies of the sutras in advance and invite the great multitude to read them at their leisure (for this assembly, there is one scroll titled "Opening the Gate of Ambrosia"; please proceed according to it; it is not provided here again).
The Discourse for the Exchange of Salutations between Host and Guest upon the Conclusion of the Retreat.

(The Host says: On this day of the early autumn month, during the observance of the proper season, I respectfully wish that [Name] may enjoy three generations of auspicious fortune and ever continue to receive your gracious favor.
The holy decree has been completed. During this long summer retreat, I have greatly burdened you with my dependence upon your support; I am fortunate that no demonic afflictions have occurred.

It is my hope that your reputation shall spread across the lakes and seas, and your Way shall be disseminated throughout the monastic groves, far fulfilling the hearts of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and forever satisfying the aspirations of devas and humans.
Your humble servant cannot overcome the utmost sincerity of his prayers.

(The guest says: This very day (as before). I, a solitary and ignorant person, have received your compassionate protection to the highest degree. During these ninety days of the ritual retreat, how much have I looked up to your virtue!

Now that the long summer has come to an end, I only hope that your fame and virtue may advance together, and that your spiritual merit and worldly blessings may both be honored. (He strikes the gavel.)
You have swept through renowned monasteries and spread the light of wisdom throughout this degenerate age. Your humble servant cannot contain the utmost sense of honor and fortune.
August and September.
The furnace is opened on the first day of the tenth month.
On the fifth day is the anniversary of the Great Master Bodhidharma; on this day, offerings are prepared and an altar is set up, and the abbot serves tea and soup.
Perform prostrations. Recite the Śūraṅgama Mantra and perform the dedication of merit.

On the winter solstice of the eleventh month, there shall be recitations at the Local Deity Hall during the winter nights and the formal lectures for the winter morning (the details of these matters are contained in the Annual Regulations).

On the first day of the twelfth month is the anniversary of Master Gaofeng’s passing. Regarding the offerings, the chanting of sutras, and other rites, their scale— whether lavish or modest— should be established according to the means of those who perform them.
The eighth day of the first month: the Buddha attained enlightenment (the events of this day are fully recorded in the *Nirvāṇa* section; they are not repeated here).
Year-end ritual for the recitation at the Local Deity Hall (*Jishidi-táng*).
Annual regulations.
Three people constitute a community. Once these words have been spoken, they must be put into practice. The regulations for a year ought to be prepared in advance;

since this matter concerns the establishment of a foundation, its accomplishment necessarily depends upon diligent effort. For one month, with utmost sincerity, the Amitāyus Dharma-hall shall be opened;
for ninety days, through cultivation and realization, the Śūraṅgama Buddha-activities shall be proclaimed. Since the assembly has gathered in a single hermitage, [they shall perform] the rites...
One may leave the four seasonal offerings empty; the handle of the ladle for mixing vinegar and minced meat—how could one allow the mind to dwell upon it after the search has already been made?
To plant the moon and hoe the clouds, one must possess the eye before the first excrement has even fallen.
In a single moment of mental awakening, the myriad paths share the same way; this is precisely the identity of phenomena and principle.
The sacred festival is inaugurated on the [day] of the [month]. Incense, candles, tea, and fruit are prepared in advance as offerings.

Three to five days prior, the ceremonial placards, petitions, and sūtra lists are written. On the morning of the actual day, the bell and wooden board are struck to assemble the assembly. The abbot emerges and burns incense.
Insert one incense stick. Offer one bowl of tea. Insert another incense stick. Withdraw slightly and, together with the assembly, perform three prostrations facing the Buddha.
Upon rising, recite the memorial (shu). Having finished the recitation, chant the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī. The procedure for the concluding distribution on this day is the same;

however, at the time of the concluding distribution, as the assembly rises from their prostrations, they immediately chant the sutra. When the sutra is finished, at the very end, recite [the memorial].
Commentary: Within this month, every day at the break of dawn, the assembly shall chant the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* and perform the dedication for the longevity of the Emperor.
After the morning gruel, the monks take turns before the Buddha to set out a scripture table and read the texts.
When it is time for the evening *can*, the bell is struck and they descend from the hall. Each day when ascending to the hall, the bell is likewise struck. The abbot hears the bell twice daily.
Upon hearing the call, one ascends the hall to burn incense. Each day, the administrative office (kūsī) prepares tea and fruit to offer to those ascending the hall;
this is because both superiors and subordinates alike manifest their sincerity.
The "Four Seasons" (Sìjié) of the ancient monastic regulations were regarded as the most significant events of the year.

These four seasons refer to the commencement of the retreat (*jiézhì*), the conclusion of the retreat (*jièzhì*), the winter solstice (*dōngzhì*), and the New Year (*suìcháo*). In recent times, these have mostly been treated as secular festivals; only the [monastic] lectures...
Regarding the rituals for the commencement and conclusion of the retreat (jie-zhi), our monastery should likewise follow these precedents. However, we cannot fully implement all the formal functions.

For instance, while various monasteries produce charts, registers, and draft lists, and specially prepare tea and soup upon the commencement of the retreat, these practices should all be dispensed with here at the hermitage.
We shall only prepare large incense and candles in advance on the thirteenth day of the fourth lunar month.
Flower, fruit, and tea offerings were arranged before the Buddha. The *Śūraṅgama* Assembly was inaugurated for ninety days and concluded on the thirteenth day of the seventh month;
both the opening and the conclusion were accompanied by formal petitions and proclamations to acknowledge the power of the divine spirits’ forest-like protection.

On the evening of the fourteenth, during the evening service (*sāyam-pātha*), recitations were performed before the Local Deity (*sthānapati*), followed by the arrangement of ritual offerings at the Hall of the Monastic Protector (*ārāmika*). I have used...

To repay the merit of guarding and cultivating realization for ninety days: on the morning of the fifteenth day of the fourth month, the assembly gathers to chant the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* and offer prayers for the Emperor.
Upon the completion of the dedication of merit, the abbot and the head seat stand facing each other, while the two orders of monks from the east and west wings stand in their respective positions.
The abbot and the head seat each take out a piece of incense and place it upon the burner. (The practitioner shouts:
"The abbot, the head seat, and the assembly perform three prostrations with full prostration (*chuli*) to mark the ceremony of the commencement of the retreat (*jie-zhi*).

Having risen from their bows and finished the seasonal greetings, the abbot, the head seat, and the assembly each take their seats in a circle. (If there is no head seat, simply invite the hall master.)
Those of middle age or seniority shall take their place [in the hall]. The practitioners of the *xingtang* (hall-walking) line up in front.

When the head practitioner (*candou*) reaches the incense burner, he inserts incense and performs three prostrations together with the assembly, then rises. The head practitioner leads the practitioners to first pay respects before the abbot.
Next, they proceed to circumambulate and pay respects before the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) and the rest of the assembly, completing one circuit and then withdrawing. At the hermitage...
The Abbot rises and burns a single stick of incense. After bowing to the Head Seat and the assembly, he serves a cup of hot water.
Once this is finished, everyone rises to thank him for the water and withdraws. All matters concerning protocol between seniors and juniors are contained within these proceedings.

Each person returns to their own seat in the bowl-row to eat porridge; no further formalities or greetings are exchanged. This is because the affairs of a mountain retreat must be simple and concise. [End of] the lifting of the retreat.
The same applies to these rituals.

Whether one performs the rites of the winter solstice and the New Year’s audience or not depends entirely on the individual; it simply does not go beyond this. Thus, one should calculate the year accordingly.
Cultivating fields is a matter of one year’s provision; tending vegetable gardens is likewise a matter of one year’s provision. How could the principles for managing one’s livelihood be disregarded?

Among the ancients, there were those who "plowed the fields to provide ample food" and those who "opened up fields to explain the Great Meaning," as well as the tradition of planting while holding a hoe or standing with hands folded.
Furthermore, both Guankui and Chan Master Ji served as gardeners (*yuántóu*); their enduring legacy continues to flourish and spread the Way.

The resonance is full. Yet, as the Dharma endures for long, decay arises. When the custom of those high and low seeking only ease and security has flourished, even those who occupy their posts merely to collect their rations give rise to sighs and grievances;
how could they know that at the edge of the mattock lies the principle of attaining Buddhahood in this very standing?

For this reason, I have established this mountain retreat to emulate the ancients. Since there is the urgent need for food and clothing, I dare not seek the comfort of my physical form. Thus, I have composed these rules.

Share their labor; when they rest, share their ease. Although one may not be able to assist with the plow or carry the spade, one must still provide meals and hot water, ensuring that the workers know that these efforts are for their own sake.
Thus, Baizhang established the precept: "If you do not work for a day, you shall not eat for a day.
How could this be in vain? As for the tools used for tilling the fields and cultivating the gardens, their edges must be kept sharp and well-tempered.

The blade is truly sharpened upon its handle, its mechanism made supple and agile, and its edge made lush and abundant. Thus, there is no failure in what is undertaken, and every year there is a harvest of achievement.
This is secretly aided by the power of the Way and far assisted by superior causes; it is the fundamental basis for manifesting the truth and returning to the source. How could this be neglected?
Furthermore, once one's labors are complete, one must be prepared for further cultivation. As for "cultivation," it refers to encountering...

During the dog days of summer, one should prepare fermented soy sauce, vinegar, and fermented beans; gather pepper blossoms, dry melons and eggplants, and set aside grain for fermentation and brining.
One must seek out the methods for these brewing processes and adopt the most excellent ones as a model.
By doing so, the products will not be spoiled and will satisfy many palates. Furthermore, all vessels and implements used for these purposes must be carefully guarded and maintained at all times.
Store [these items] so that they do not become defiled; this is also an unavoidable requirement for the annual budget. Therefore, I have recorded this and appended it here.

Since the affairs of Shifan’an have been made manifest, the ritual protocols must necessarily be complete. Whether for prayers of averting calamity, petitions for blessings, expressions of gratitude, or celebratory consolations, the performance of the rites is indeed essential.

Regarding sincerity, matters involve literary elegance; thus, monasteries appoint secretaries and recorders whose compositions are refined and classical to delight both the eyes and ears, so that they may serve as models for the world and ensure the long endurance of the Dharma.
The monastic community at the sacred festival altar shall peruse this;
the catalog of various sutras for the single-volume format follows below.
The Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra; the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra on the Sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna;
and the Mahāvaipulya Samantabhadra-bodhicitta-uttaratantra-sūtra-nītārtha (The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment of the Great Vehicle, Explaining the Definitive Meaning).
The Mahāyāna Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra;
the Lotus Flower Cintāmaṇi Cakra-rāja Divine Mantra of the Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta Sūtra for the Elimination of Calamities; and the Sūtra of Praise.
The title "Immeasurable Life" (Amitāyus) is inscribed on the right side of the plaque;
it is respectfully dedicated as a prayer for the present Emperor’s ten-thousand-year reign and his eternal peace and well-being.
On this day of this month, the Hall of the Hermitage is fully prepared.
A Memorial for the Commencement of the Sacred Festival.
At the Huanzhu Chan Hermitage on Mount Bian, west of the city of Huzhou. Your servant-monk [Name]. On such-and-such a day of such-and-such a month, we reverently encounter the Heavenly [Festival].
At the Shoushengjie Hermitage, preparations have been made to inaugurate a one-month *Vajra-Amitāyus* Dharma assembly on the [blank] day of this month.
Each day, the monks shall take turns ascending the hall to peruse the *Golden Texts* and recite the secret mantras (*guhyamantra*).
On this day, the assembly shall open with the chanting of the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī and the extolling of the Holy Name. Thus it is recorded.

We, Hong Yin and others, hereby offer our prayers for the ten-thousand-year longevity and eternal peace of His Majesty the Emperor. On the right, we humbly submit that the imperial edict inscribed in vermilion stirs joy throughout the mountains, rivers, altars of earth, and altars of grain;
the crimson sun shines brightly across the heavens, bringing comfort to all plants, trees, insects, and creatures. We reverently approach this auspicious occasion of the Emperor’s birthday.
Devoutly honoring the Buddha Vehicle, you proclaim the essential exegesis of the secret teachings and offer prayers for the long endurance of Your Majesty’s sagacious reign.

We respectfully pray that, like the sun above and the moon below, You may radiate the brilliance of supreme and vast sagacity; and like the height of mountains and the depth of the ocean, [may Your virtue be eternal].
May the fortune and longevity of Your Most Exalted Majesty be firmly consolidated. However, we, the humble monk (Name) and others, cannot restrain our feelings of longing as we gaze upon Heaven;
our earnest hope for Your Holiness is most fervent. We are filled with the utmost trepidation. Respectfully submitted.
On the [day] of the [month] of the [year], the monk of humble rank [Name] submits this memorial.
Memorial for the Concluding Ceremony on the Imperial Birthday:

[Together we] arrive. May our merits be equal and our provisions doubled. We pray universally that whatever rain we seek may be swiftly granted through spiritual resonance.

We only wish that the clouds of compassion spread thickly and the sun of wisdom withdraws its light, pouring down a torrential sweet dew to moisten the parched sprouts so they may flourish and grow lush.

I humbly pray that the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional may be harmonized, and that concentration and wisdom may shine forth together. May the lotus of the mind blossom brilliantly, as the fragrant breeze passes through the jade trees and jeweled groves;

may the fruit of the Way be perfected, as the rain of Dharma nourishes the precious garden and the golden ground. May we gaze toward the City of Enlightenment and find the path, pointing toward the ocean of the Buddhas.
To act as a patriarch, one turns the inexhaustible wheel and attains the fruit of non-retrogression.

Realizing that the nature of the Dharma-realm is neither male nor female, the Gate of Non-duality is fully manifested everywhere. Realizing the pure essence, there is neither awakening nor delusion;
within the ocean of samādhi, every speck of dust enters in interpenetration. The Udumbara flower blooms in the Anāthapiṇḍika Garden;
the mani jewel is offered to the Treasury of Radiance. (Female usage)

the mountain of merit towers high in every atom. Birth and death are empty within their own substance; nirvana is realized within one's own mind.
In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven Palace, all together they realize Māyā; in the Immaculate World, they transcend the Dragon Girl.

grain by grain, the fruit of one’s own mind is formed. Completely transcending the outflows, they truly realize non-arising. (For men)

the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada’s Jetavana is his home, being his ancestral residence. Cultivation and realization are thus accomplished, and their fruition is manifest before one. (For men:

If before Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or Patriarchs, one says: "The extraordinary merit thus accumulated. (Before Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one says:

"Dedicate [this merit]. (Before Patriarchs, one says: "On behalf of their True Compassion. (The general title is: "Above, to repay the compassionate shade [of our parents]. (For Patriarchs alone, one says: "May their rank and position be further exalted."
Furthermore, before all the deities of the heavens and the three realms, one says: "The merit accumulated is exclusively offered as a prayer of dedication.

Regarding all deceased persons, one says: "The roots of goodness accumulated," or "victorious benefits," which are exclusively offered as a memorial service (*tsi-chan*), or "exclusively offered as a guidance through rebirth" (*chi-dao*).
[For a monk] one says: "Awakened Spirit" (*chiao-ling*); [for a man] "Divine Countenance" (*shen-i*); [for a woman] "Virtuous Lady" (*shu*).
For the *hún* (soul): "Respectfully encountering" (*gōngyù*). For the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas: "Prostrating before the encounter" (*fúyù*). For the deceased: "Now meeting" (*zīzhí*).
However, at the end of the memorial for the *zhùshèng* (prayers for the Emperor), use: "The Imperial Enlightenment, penetratingly clear, Dragon and Heaven."

In the *Fó pǔ jí shū* (Extensive Commentary on the Buddha’s Enlightenment), if [the text] includes both Buddhas and deities, it says: "The Buddha-sun shines through with clarity; the divine spirits respond with manifest resonance.
For all subsequent documents concerning various heavenly deities and luminous beings, this shall serve as the precedent. However, for all documents concerning deceased persons, it says:
"The Buddha-mind knows [this] immediately; the merit-text document. If one encounters a document for a long life (*shòu shū*), it says: "The Buddha-sun shines through with clarity; the star..."

Heavenly One, look down with clear discernment. This is respectfully submitted. As for the dedication at the two times of the vegetarian meal and the gruel, when encountering a prayer for the Emperor (one says:

"at the morning gruel and midday meal"), it is a great cause to pray for the longevity and ten-thousand-fold peace of the present Emperor. Recite the "Pure Dharma Body" [mantra] (*etc.*). [It is not permitted to say, "I rely upon..."]

The four characters for "the great assembly" (dàzhòng) and other such matters are all explained by those who understand them; however, there are differences in their significance, and these must not be confused.
This is because one must not lose the proper order of honor and humility. Furthermore, there are more subtle matters that I have no leisure to investigate further.
This cannot be fully recorded in writing; it rests entirely with each individual, who ought to examine it for themselves.
Whether it be the preparation of one's livelihood or the management of one's affairs, there is nothing that those who have taken form in this world can avoid, even in their own persons. Therefore:
In the monastic forests, there is a saying: "One sits, another walks, and seven go forth. As for satisfying hunger, one certainly does not discriminate between coarse and refined food;

as for sheltering from wind and rain, how could one dare to compare it as being shabby or lowly? One must repair [the buildings] every day; this responsibility rests with the person in charge. When a hundred flavors are presented, the merit returns to oneself.
It is hoped that by planning for the transmission through the ages and the preservation of the teachings, they may serve as a model and a standard for others. Thus...

One sees that the power to support those in peril and aid those who are falling begins and ends with purpose; its merit is not bestowed in vain. The Way exists for those who perceive it through direct observation.
[The text concludes with: *zhāi zhuàn* (Records of the Fasting Feast).
The principle of providing for the assembly rests in preparation; one should act in advance so as to avoid the urgency of the moment.

For instance, regarding the regular offerings and meals provided in the monastery, the necessary materials must be checked and accounted for frequently, ensuring that there is always a surplus for those who follow.
Should supplies prove insufficient, one must arrange for them as appropriate—either by seeking out donors or appealing to patrons. The matter requires flexibility and ingenuity; do not be rigid.

One may reveal one's tracks, or perhaps one does not wish to seek outside; on the appointed day, one should also slightly differ from the usual routine, for this is the skillful means (*upāya*) for assisting the assembly.
Furthermore, regarding the ordinary rice gruel and meals, there is certainly no need for elaborate arrangements; nevertheless, one must attend to them daily and maintain order at all times.
Skillful means are easily modified, such that one can transform frugality into abundance without causing any depletion of internal grain or wealth.

Regarding such intrusions and excesses, if one does not maintain a state of mutual regard like ice and snow toward external things, it will all depend on the application of the mind to fully accomplish superior practice.
Otherwise, how could one fulfill the responsibilities of residing in the assembly? (Alternatively, "residing" may be read as "entrusting.")
One should repair and plaster the walls and roofs of one's dwelling so that they may endure as protection against wind and rain, ensuring that no flaws such as cracks or leaks occur.
One must habitually mend what is damaged, fill what is hollow, block what is perforated, and support what has sagged, never allowing them to fall into ruin.
In time, it fell into ruin and became a collection of filth;
what was later called the "Eastern Ablution" or "Western Ablution" refers to the purity residing in the person, not in the physical site.
Various regions established the office of the *jintou* (ablution supervisor), who used towels for wiping and water for washing, as well as brooms for sweeping.
Sweep and clear away [dirt]. A lamp is used for illumination; though it may become soiled, it must always remain clean.
Now that there are no practitioners maintaining ritual purity within this mountain hermitage, anyone who performs administrative duties should pay close attention and maintain constant supervision.
Furthermore, ensure that all various utensils in the rear quarters are kept in full supply and never lacking.
The bathhouse is the place where the great assembly proclaims the wondrous touch of purity. Who can avoid washing away the dust and cleansing the defilements?
One must constantly inspect the vats, jars, buckets, ladles, stoves, cauldrons, firewood, and fuel. Ensure that the water drains and channels are not obstructed.

To open up clarity and manifest purity in order to delight the minds of the assembly: there will surely be those who cast down the tally-sticks and lift up the ladle-head who attain sudden enlightenment.
Zhaozhou’s “The toilet is not a place for preaching the Buddha-dharma” was a divine mechanism of transcendent ease;
Guling’s act of rubbing his master’s back was a wondrous function of the Unconditioned. To repay such effortless practice—how could it be a minor contribution?
Always keep the path before the hermitage clear and open. Always ensure that the rooms and quarters within the hermitage are orderly and secure.
Always exercise great care in protecting the wind and candles beneath the hearth. Always maintain the ritual implements before the Buddha with precision and solemnity.

Do not let the lamp illuminating the night grow dim; do not neglect the fire used to ward off the cold. Paste paper on the windows, wipe the vessels, sweep the floors, and prepare the incense. Weed out the grass and trim the fences.
Carrying firewood and fetching water, these activities do not hinder the application of the Way and also assist in the practice of the gate of cultivation.
Those who have mastered their original nature and dwell in mountain huts are ones who see that the ancient style has not yet fallen into ruin.
In this family tradition, companions walk shoulder-to-shoulder without the need for frequent blows or shouts. Fellow practitioners extend their hands to bid them set down their bowls.
Within a flash of lightning, the host and guest are clearly verified; before the skull, rewards and punishments are secretly administered. The royal road lies within oneself.
In essence, it is only valued when the eye is intimate and the hand is prompt. Opening the door to await those of true knowledge, it is indeed as the saying goes: "The Way is propagated by man.

Thus, the established style of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is displayed, and fresh regulations for the monastic groves are laid out. Rather than merely holding the almsbowl to beg for sustenance, [one must act with such immediacy].
How is it that while plowing fields and sowing rice, one seeks to bring supreme practice to full perfection? We all must exert ourselves together;

though my original intention in settling here in this hermitage was to dwell in solitude, there is now a fellow seeker who has come from afar wishing to rely upon me. Such a person must possess proper dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*).
One should request to stay before the abbot of the hermitage according to the formal procedures for seeking lodging at various monasteries; one must not act with haste.

If the abbot wishes to accept you, he shall personally escort you back to the hall. There, you and the newly arrived monk shall take your positions as guest and host within the hall and perform a single prostration with full touching of the ground.
The newly arrived monk then escorts the abbot back to his quarters and proceeds to pay his respects in turn to the Head Seat (shouzuo) and the assembly.
Carrying incense, one proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters and performs a prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*chuli*) to express gratitude for being granted lodging.
Regarding those who seek lodging, one must assess whether their bedding and seating are available and observe whether the newcomer is established in the Way or not.
However, even in a mountain hermitage of five or seven rooms, the ears and eyes of the residents are inevitably within reach of one another.

If the minds of those dwelling there are not set upon the Way, then at the slightest occurrence that does not accord with their wishes, discord will arise. This is because a practitioner of the Way must let go of everything within the mind.
I shall by no means allow this to circulate among the worldly. Whenever those who are not practitioners of the Way arrive, they should merely be received with courtesy and respect;
if one does not wish for them to remain, one should simply use skillful means to dismiss them, so that there may be no appearance of discrimination.

Once all those who have taken up residence in the hall have settled, the officers shall constantly prepare and manage matters such as providing for and settling the assembly, ensuring that no one dwelling there is troubled by anxious thoughts.
Should anyone from the hall go to the administrative office (kusi) to request anything, the officers must respond with tact and flexibility;
in this way, they will be seen to comfort the hearts of the assembly.
When welcoming a newly arrived guest into the hall, one performs a prostration with unraised hands (*chuli*) and stands to address the master, saying:
"This mountain hermitage is secluded and its surroundings are desolate; that we may forget ourselves through the Way brings me boundless joy. The guest replies:
"Now that I have been accepted into this community, I have finally found a place to settle. To attend upon you morning and evening, how could it be anything but a source of supreme honor?"
○ Regarding the expression of gratitude for being granted a berth, the guest says to the abbot:
"I ought to have seen you off earlier; as my courtesy was insufficient, I am deeply moved and ashamed that you have nonetheless deigned to visit me."

The guest said: "I have just been honored by your gracious reception, which has exceeded all formal courtesy. I am unable to offer my thanks in person; I humbly hope for your compassionate forgiveness.
Your hermitage is secluded and remote, inaccessible by the paths of the world. Wearing rain-cloaks and carrying smoke-wrapped bundles, we have come seeking your gate—sometimes three, sometimes five."

Gratefully acknowledging your gracious visit, incense and candles are prepared at the entrance of the hermitage. Waiting for [the guest] to wash his feet and assume the proper dignified demeanor, the host welcomes him with formal greetings and bows him into a seat.

Once the burning of incense is complete, they bow again. After the serving of tea is finished, the guest rises to express thanks for the tea. The host then proceeds to escort him to his quarters to settle in.
Although the guest quarters may not be spacious, one must provide beds, mats, bedding, curtains, and seating as appropriate.

The etiquette regarding tea, soup, snacks, and fruit offerings must not be treated with negligence; rather, they should simply accord with the family’s means, whether abundant or modest. As the ancients said:
"If human relations are good, even drinking water makes one fat. It is in the ritual propriety, not in the material objects, that the essence lies.
The teachings state that when visiting monks arrive at a monastery, they should be provided with various offerings;

just as when there is an invitation from a patron, one must first invite the visiting monks, otherwise one commits a transgression. Now that you have established the incense and lamps of a particular locality, you should prioritize welcoming and receiving guests.
Since both parties are dwelling together within the ocean of the Buddha’s Dharma, you should ensure that you do not fall into the reproach of being callous toward those who follow behind.
When employing people for a mountain hermitage with the intent to manifest the traditional style of one's own house, it is impossible to lack personnel for all matters.
However, when wishing to employ them, one must carefully examine their capabilities and observe what they find comfortable. In the present age, those who employ people often seek only—
At such times of managing affairs, one must investigate whether the person's inner intent is sincere or hypocritical. If their heart is set on truth, they may be employed even if they are clumsy;
if their mind dwells on hypocrisy, they must not be associated with even if they are clever.
If one values versatile talent for a mere moment, one will surely facilitate deceit and disorder for a long time. How can one not be careful when employing others?
The advancement or retirement of the worthy and the unworthy through reward and punishment depends on whether those rewards and punishments are impartial or not.

When rewards and punishments are impartial, even ten thousand people do not appear to be too many. When rewards and punishments are not impartial, even a single person cannot bring about good governance.
This is the principle of impartiality. Once it is established, the worthy need not be summoned to advance, and the unworthy need not be censured to withdraw.
As for those who are unworthy, they will not merely withdraw; there will be among them those who, admiring my virtuous and enlightened Way, will reform themselves.
This is how transformation occurs without words: those nearby are pleased, and those afar are drawn. It is not through rewards and punishments.

How, then, did you, my lord, attain this? Yet dwelling in a hermitage is the business of a man of the Way. Therein, there is no honor from jade or silk for rewards, nor any disgrace of legal punishment for penalties;
rather, the substance of reward and penalty consists simply in whether one draws others near or keeps them at a distance.

Now, as for those who have merit and deserve reward, one should treat them with increasingly greater intimacy and respect. As for those who have transgressions and deserve punishment, one should merely use skillful means to encourage their reform.

If he disregards his own kin, one should treat him as a relative if he follows one's advice; however, if he does not comply despite repeated exhortation, one should simply distance oneself from him gradually day by day so that he may reflect upon himself.
Should one instead show him special favor, it will certainly cause injury to compassion and is most certainly not the way to harmonize the community.

Advancing and retreating, primary and secondary elements intermingle; there are distinctions between union and separation. Meeting on devious paths, going and staying depend upon conditions. In principle, one cannot be dogmatic;
in practice, there is no fixed doctrine. As for those who manage affairs within the hermitage, whether for a year or three to five years, it depends upon their mental and physical strength.
If one becomes fatigued and wishes to request leave to return to the hall to join the assembly, the presiding official should repeatedly exhort them to remain and comply with the conditions.

If their resolve is firm and they will not comply, they should be permitted to withdraw as they wish. The abbot shall ring the bell for the assembly’s tea to see them off, whether to the quarters or the hall.
Once they have been sent off, one or two days later, a single banquet of refreshments must be prepared to await them; this is a rare instance of receiving recompense.

This is the ritual for laboring [in the community]. If one wishes to request someone to fill the office of a predecessor, one must first have a close acquaintance privately and confidentially negotiate with them.
Only when they have given their consent should the tea for the assembly be announced. The Abbot says:

"Since such-and-such a person has retired from this office, this duty must not be left without personnel. I now request that such-and-such a person fill it; I look forward to the compassion of the assembly to join me in this."
The formal invitation is extended. The abbot and the assembly together perform a single prostration with touching of the forehead (*chuli*) toward the person invited.
The invitee also bows. They then proceed together with the assembly to escort him back to his office.

Once the congratulations have been concluded, the newly appointed official shall immediately carry incense and visit the abbot’s quarters to express his gratitude. On the following day, the public community shall prepare a single banquet of refreshments.
Please have the administrative officers accompany you to demonstrate the courtesy of hosting.
Whether the abbot has passed away, is exhausted, or wishes to retire due to illness, he should inform the donor of these circumstances and request that they seek a successor as soon as possible.
Once a replacement has been found, the former incumbent should notify the assembly several days in advance of his retirement.
Whether one goes to another's home or resides in a quiet room within the monastery, the attendant in charge of the monastery must prepare incense, candles, and offerings for the meal.
Alternatively, they may inform neighboring households and patrons (*dānapati*), who shall bring fragrant offerings to the new resident’s quarters to pay their respects.

He was informed to request an auspicious day for entering the hermitage. It was advised that he should prepare various kinds of solemn decorations; the rites of welcome must not be perfunctory or simplified.
He must provide offerings of food and drink, hold a gathering with neighboring lords, and present generous *dakṣiṇā* (offerings) to the new abbot as a token of congratulation.
Furthermore, he must present generous *dakṣiṇā* to the former residents as a token of gratitude. Only then should the new abbot personally visit neighboring lords and donors to pay his respects.
Upon paying their respects, the former abbot shall also proceed in turn to the households of lay patrons in neighboring districts to express his gratitude.
In this way, it will be seen that both the advancing and the retreating are each conducted with propriety.

During the time of the Buddha, although his assembly numbered as many as one thousand two hundred and fifty members, it was never heard that they established extensive fields or constructed large residences.
Whenever mealtime arrived, each would take his appropriate alms-bowl and enter various villages to wander from house to house begging for food. This was their practice of begging for sustenance.
They dwelt wherever they found shelter—in rocky caves and forest groves. Yet, in the final five hundred years, social customs will become corrupt;
people will reside in ornate houses and subsist on fertile lands, caring only for the gratification of their mouths and bodies, while failing to investigate the source of birth and death.

Those who beg for food destroy the stinginess and greed of others and subdue their own pride; they do not seek to provide for themselves first, but desire to benefit others. Thus, one should go from door to door.
When going on almsround, one should constantly reflect that sentient beings are weighed down by the heavy defilements of stinginess and greed, drowning in the river of craving.

Relying upon my transformative power, I shall cause them to give; whether the gift be much or little, all are fields of merit. Whether encountering joy or anger, do not give rise to hatred or attachment.
He expands his vow of universal equality and gives rise to unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-maitrī*). The worlds of the ten directions are all gates of giving (*dāna*);
all men and women are equally called donors (*dānapati*). Benefiting both self and others alike, they mutually support one another through the dharma of food.

They strike down from afar the dense forest of stinginess, greed, delusion, and anger, and mount high upon the leisurely carriage of liberation and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Formerly, when Master Cishou sent away a master of alms-gathering, he composed a verse:
It is said: "Lightly drifting with a single bowl, he enters the imperial capital; ten thousand households and a thousand gates present a most extraordinary scene.

On another day, passing beneath three rafter-beams, he will likely not distinguish between the quality of the morning gruel and the midday meal. Although these words are brief, they certainly do not fall short of the teachings on Yangshan’s rice.
Thus we know that begging for alms with a bowl is the fundamental practice, never shifting from beginning to end, of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Should students...
If one refrains from practicing out of a dread of lowliness, then there is no distinction between such a person and the non-Buddhists.

There are those who, though their robes and bowls are not in surplus and their food and drink are unrestricted, know only to rely on these as causes for seeking profit; they fail to realize that by pursuing the delusive, they are creating the fruit of repaying debts.

Their names may be identical to those of the noble practices, yet their traces differ from the true source. Thus, the paths of ascent and descent diverge, and the gates of benefit and harm are opened.
Indeed! Should one not take this as a warning? Should one not take this as a warning?

All places where the community dwells in peace are necessarily accomplished through the collective labor of the multitude. As for tending the hearth, carrying out grain, pounding rice, and clearing the fallow fields—these too depend upon the same effort.

In carrying earth, there was once the custom of communal labor (*fushō*). In recent times, however, people have engaged in this work with extravagance, employing servants for the task and transforming diligent toil into idle ease.
Younger generations have become accustomed to this, turning it into a prevailing custom; they ruin the true cause and waste their years in vain.
What can these ignorant folk hope for as they grow old? Now, at this mountain hermitage, I strive to emulate the ancient style. Or...
When repairing houses or buildings, one may personally prepare the vegetarian offerings, select fruits and vegetables, or transport firewood and fuel.
Since there are no servants to take over such labor, one must rely entirely upon the manual efforts of others. Yet, every bit of this work ultimately returns to oneself;

it is clear that merit is never bestowed in vain. Fearing that one’s own exertion might be incomplete, how could one ever reproach others for being insatiable? This is precisely what constitutes spiritual practice.
This is the correct standard and the common path for entering the Way.
"Name" (ming) refers to that which is designated; "designation" (fen) refers to the actual phenomena (dharmas) summoned by the name. Not yet...
There are parts without names; how could there be names without parts?

To trace their origin, all ten dharma realms are "names," while within those dharma realms, awakening and delusion, good and evil, suffering and joy, rising and sinking, are all "parts. For example, the name "fire" must necessarily possess the part of its nature that is heat.
Now, in the monastic communities, names are established according to circumstances, and through these names, the reality is revealed.

The distinctions between heavy and light, and the differences in excellence, are appropriately established; through this, one's meritorious practice becomes perfected, and the Way of the Dharma is thereby made manifest.
— The Abbot.
Now, one who serves as the abbot of a hermitage is the elder of the monastic community. He is like the beam of a house, the rudder of a ship, or the crossbar of a scale.
In all matters at the gate of the hermitage—whether taking or rejecting, or whatever activities are undertaken—one must first deliberate them within the mind.
If one cannot decide for oneself, one must consult others who have experienced many affairs and possess mature wisdom. There is no matter too great.
In the first year of Xiaoshao, the principle of public service was paramount. Indeed, the single word "public" (gong) is that upon which the boundaries of governance depend.

If even a single thought does not dwell upon the public, one will see the superior leading from above and the subordinates emulating from below; once private interest prevails, then even if one constantly stores grain in quantities as vast as mountains, it will be of no avail.
Then its decline and ruin will arrive without even waiting for an invitation. One need not worry that material affairs will not be abundant;
one should only worry that the ruler’s mind does not abide in impartiality (*gong*). If the impartial heart is not obscured, then the empty can become substantial and the weak can become strong.

Nearby, those who have yet to arrive will submit with joy; afar, dragons and spirits will provide protection. What is called "impartiality" means that the mind dwells upon the multitude rather than oneself.

This depends on oneself. Whenever facing a matter or responding to circumstances, one should not weigh things according to the distinction between the near and the distant, nor should one grant or withhold based on feelings of love or hatred.
One must ensure that every affair is perfectly integrated and that every phenomenon is met with skillful means.

Even when encountering matters that contradict one's sentiments or violate reason, one should handle them with broadmindedness and generosity, solely by way of protecting the good and obstructing the evil.
To cause injury to compassion in a single thought is most certainly not the great principle of being a leader.
As for the title "Head Seat" (Shouzuo), it signifies one who dwells at the head of the assembly; within the monastic community, he shares the beauty of wind and moon with the Elder Abbot.

Within the hermitage, he shared in the monastic duties with the abbot. His affairs were characterized by diligent application; his conduct remained pure and pristine; he forgot both hatred and affection;
and his thoughts were severed from right and wrong. He was the embodiment of the standards for the ten directions and the locus upon which the spiritual cultivation of the entire assembly depended.
Whether striking the board for a formal sitting, concluding a period of meditation, or engaging in various activities of movement and stillness, nothing escapes his concern.

He is ever apprehensive that his conditions for the Way have not yet been discerned or that his Dharma-activity has not reached all. Should there be those among the assembly who are indolent, he must urge them toward diligent effort;

should there be those who violate the communal rules, he must restrain them with broad magnanimity. Furthermore, the regulations for a mountain hermitage are not comparable to those of a great monastic center. Regarding all matters of etiquette—

Whether the provisions for the kitchen and hall are abundant or meager, all matters are moderated with impartiality. Constantly maintaining the resolve to rely on fire-seeds and slash-and-burn cultivation, one’s life and shadow shall be companions in solitude;
thus, one naturally does not fall into the ways of the present age. The application of the Way lies therein.
The assistant abbot (fu-ʼan) manages the affairs of the single abbot (yi-ʼan). The primary master is like the body; the assistant who supports that master is like the body having arms.
"Assistant" (fu) means to aid; it refers to assisting the principal so as not to allow him to become biased or deviant. Whenever the abbot errs...

Regarding deliberation and the execution of practice, one should provide timely reminders and engage in private consultation so that the public way may daily flourish and the primary cause may daily manifest.
Through this, administrative affairs will be brought to equilibrium and ritual laws will be properly applied.
Should the abbot be away and a matter arise before you, whatever you perform by proxy must take due measure of the principal’s disposition.

One must respond with flexibility and adaptability; it is improper to insist solely on one's own views while failing to accord with the master’s sentiments, for this is by no means the mark of a capable assistant.
However, if one continues to serve for a long time, the master’s authority will eventually devolve [to the assistant].

As an assistant, if one does not obstruct the master’s intentions, then not only will there be harmony between superior and subordinate, but in the future, there will surely be those who, unable to restrain their talent, will follow in succession to provide excellent assistance. This is...
This means that when the form is straight, the shadow is upright. Viewed from this perspective, it is not that one conforms to the master, but rather that one conforms to oneself.
Those who place themselves beneath the constraints of rank and duty ought to reflect upon this.
It is known that in ancient monasteries there was no title for "Vice-Kitchen Steward" (Fu-si); they were simply called "Kūtòu" (Storehouse Head).

This office managed all receipts, expenditures, and internal affairs, which is precisely the function of the Kitchen Steward. All items belonging to the storehouse administration—whether gold, grain, or monastery equipment—without exception, regardless of their size, were recorded in writing.
Regarding the ledgers: the ancients said that one should cherish and protect communal property as if guarding the jewel in one's eye. When it pertains to daily use, it is termed "fruit and cause";

when it pertains to future retribution, it becomes "sin or merit. As for all items provided for the assembly—such as rice, wheat, oil, flour, sauce, vinegar, tea, and salt—one must inspect them frequently and keep them stored with constant mindfulness.
One must guard against insect infestation and prevent them from becoming moldy or spoiled.
Furthermore, regarding wealth, silk, and all utensils used, one must collect them at the appropriate time and not allow them to be discarded.

This ensures that they can be handed over with ease when the time comes; otherwise, all matters will be neglected and forgotten. Having thus failed in one's sincerity toward the community, it will be difficult to escape retribution after death.
Consider the ancients among the venerable masters who spread their glorious reputations and accomplished sublime practices, such as those who used large bowls and precious ginger.
The lineage of Dharma Master Shenzhao took this as a provisional path; it is indeed the staircase for becoming a Buddha and a Patriarch.

At the very moment one weighs and calculates [the mind], it is truly the shortcut to the emptiness of the heart that passes the imperial examination. If one says that worldly toil and entanglements bind one, [one fails to see this].
Know that he is not a man of the true cause. Reflect upon this, reflect upon it!
The rice gruel served by the head cook is that which sustains the very life-vein of the entire assembly; one must therefore pay careful attention to this matter. Thus, in the monastic groves—
From the chief cook (*karmadāna*) down to the receptionist, there are approximately several dozen people who all serve as officials responsible for providing the five flavors for the two daily meals;
this is the path of public duty. Now, in a mountain hermitage (*āśrama*), only one head cook is appointed to manage these affairs in their entirety.
All those who assume this responsibility must with earnest diligence regard the food as the sustenance of the great assembly.

They must observe the timing of the meal—whether it is early or late—and weigh the number of those who will eat. They must inspect the quality of the rice and grain—whether it is fine or coarse—and distinguish between the clarity or turbidity of the water and broth.
They must exercise restraint regarding the quantity of vegetables and take heed of whether firewood is available, even down to the collection [of refuse].
Wash and cleanse [the vessels] so as not to allow them to become defiled or to spoil through stagnation. If the food is insufficient, the practitioners' sustenance will not be sufficient;
if it is excessive, what benefit is there in its being discarded? Ensure that the raw and the cooked are properly balanced, and that the salty and the bland are harmonized.

If one day you do not disturb the minds of the assembly, you will accumulate blessings for the life hereafter throughout ten thousand ages. However, the practice of those who have left the household life is to benefit others.

This present duty is to adorn and protect the community, to comfort the minds of the multitude, and to assist in turning the wheel of food to provide distant support for the transformation of the Dharma;

it is truly the ultimate means of benefiting others. Such were the venerable elders of the past—Xuefeng, Dashi, and Miaoxi—who from this very practice ascended high to the rank of patriarchs and widely disseminated their legacy.
How could this be called a lowly or trivial matter? It is that which possesses power within the Way.
One should examine this carefully.

The practice of appointing officials to the east and west corridors according to their respective capacities is a long-standing tradition within the monastic community. Now, for those residing in hermitages, it is appropriate...
Be concise; one must not establish too many formal titles and divisions to confuse the essential spirit of the Way.

For matters such as dedicating merit (*pariṇāmanā*), making proclamations, or welcoming and seeing off guests, since there is neither a *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master) nor a guest master (*kṣetrajña*), the abbot’s assistant (*pò-ān*) may suffice to perform these duties on their behalf.

Alternatively, the abbot or the head seat (*śrīmad-ācārya*) may act according to what is appropriate and convenient, and these roles may be interchanged as needed. Or, when a donor has a religious service (*buddha-karman*) and issues a command, the abbot [shall attend].

The head seat and the others should mutually recommend someone capable to take on this role; provided that they do not lose the proper decorum of transformation, this will serve to adorn the Dharma community.

Alternatively, if the assembly yearns for the transformative influence of the Dharma and offers an incense offering as an invitation, the abbot, head seat, and others should likewise respond to one another in turn.

Relying solely upon my own observations and learning, I have endeavored to comply with the earnest entreaties of those who come to me, offering guidance as appropriate and deliberating with straightforward sincerity;
this is merely intended to provide mutual admonition. One must strictly avoid indulging in groundless speculation or critiquing the ancients and the present.
To obscure one's own mind and blind the eyes of those who study is not as good as following the precedent of not conforming to others, but instead investigating the mind for oneself.

The natural style of one's own fundamental portion is inherently extraordinary. Once the innate truth is revealed, you will realize that when the meditation cushion is crossed, the Zen board is struck, the napkin is spread, and the rice bowl is opened for a meal, these are all moments when the Great Dharma Wheel turns.
Indeed, this does not even depend upon waving a fly-whisk or sitting in a formal posture.
