The great assembly shall recite the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times. [Recite the names of] the Four Holy Ones three times each.

[Recite] the *śabda* [mantra]. Dedicate the merit (*pariṇāmana*) [as follows]: We humbly pray that for such-and-such person, may all conditions that have not yet been severed quickly lead to peace and ease;
though the great destiny is difficult to evade, may they be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nourishment (*Sukhāvatī*). [Recite] the verses on the ten directions and three periods of time, etc.

To escort one from life is joy; to mourn one’s death is sorrow. When the forest enters nirvana and the coffin reveals the twin lotus feet, the illusory form is consumed by self-kindled fire—where can it be found?
These are but ancient traces from two thousand years ago, remaining for eighty-four thousand kalpas.
Remains: A homeless guest left behind in the thickets. Since all possess a body, who among us can escape this fate?
Within the pine-casket and plain curtains, where the tiles are inscribed and the lamp is blue, these matters must be prepared in advance; the rites ought to be complete.

From the auctioning and chanting for robes and bowls to the disbursing and collecting of bedding and tents—since there is no distinction between life and death, how can one remain ignorant of cause and effect? Let us together proceed toward the Way.
Together we must return to the true source; thus the meaning of death and birth becomes clear, and the merit of establishing transformation is complete.
If a deceased monk is able to bathe and change his robes himself, he shall sit and pass away, after which he is immediately placed in the coffin for veneration.
If he is gravely ill and unable to conclude the process on his own, one must wait for his breath to cease before providing hot water and informing the Head Seat and fellow countrymen.
He bathes and puts on his robes. Regarding the method for donning the robes, it matters not whether it be winter or summer;
there are simply one waistcoat of old cloth, one bathing skirt, and a pair of old socks.

Above these, he wears one shirt of old cloth and one *zhiduō* (straight-cut robe) of old cloth, along with a head-covering net and a common rosary string. Having thus shaved his beard and hair and adjusted his attire, he enters.

The remains are placed in the shrine (*kaṅ*). Once the inventory of the remaining *kāṣāya*, alms bowl, and various travel effects has been finalized, on the day of the removal from the shrine, the money and goods are appraised and auctioned;
the proceeds are entered into the accounts for collection and disbursement to cover the expenses of the funeral procession. Regarding the method of entering the shrine:

one must prepare hemp, bamboo strips, and similar materials in advance and place them beneath the two internal organs of the deceased monk. Next, dry firewood is used to support the sides on all four directions.

Once the arrangements have been finalized, the shrine (kaṅ) shall be closed using long wooden strips joined together. The shrine door must be sealed with the official seal and the handprint of the presiding official.

In front of the shrine, a spirit tablet (wei-pan) shall be erected, inscribed as follows: "The Awakening Spirit of the Newly Deceased [Name], Former Head Monk. Incense, lamps, and candles shall be lit;
it is requested that the Head Seat and the assembly recite the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī once and dedicate the merit.

In commemoration of the merit of reciting the sutras for the newly deceased Elder [Name], as he is being placed into his coffin, we adorn the ground of retribution throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time... (and so forth).
Once the remains had been placed in the shrine, the arrangements were immediately made. Four large paper banners were cut; on them was inscribed the Verse on Impermanence:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss. These were hung beside the shrine.
Two vases with willow branches were set out, and curtains and canopies were arranged as appropriate for the occasion. Three times each day, offerings were made according to the public custom.
Having offered gruel and rice as an offering, the assembly recites the Great Compassion Mantra at each of the three periods of the day, dedicating the merit by saying:

"The merit of reciting this scripture is respectfully dedicated to the enlightened spirit of the newly deceased Elder [Name], so that his realm of retribution may be adorned. Throughout the ten directions... (and so forth).

During the three periods of the day, they recited the sutras. The villagers also chanted the Great Compassion Mantra once. The head of the village stood before the coffin and burned incense, while the last of the villagers raised the sutra for the dedication of merit.
The shrine remains until the third day. The public community prepares sacrificial food and offerings of the five flavors. At evening, the recitation begins.

During the time of the recitation, the bell and chime are struck and the wooden board is clapped as the assembly gathers. The abbot comes forth to burn incense, offer hot water and tea, and present the food;

having finished, he withdraws and performs three prostrations. Immediately thereafter, the recitation proceeds. In various traditions, the two orders of the monastic community come forward from their ranks to burn incense at the abbot’s shrine.
Regarding the practice of recitation while residing [in the monastery], it is said:
"In all earnestness, life and death alternate and cold and heat shift in succession. Their coming is like lightning flashing across the vast sky;
their departure is like waves subsiding in the great ocean. On this day, there is a newly passed-away Elder named [Name], whose karmic conditions..."
Having exhausted his great life span, he suddenly passed away. Realizing that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, he attained the bliss of nirvāṇa.
We respectfully assemble the great assembly to solemnly proceed to the funerary shrine, chanting the sublime names of the various sages to dedicate his refined spirit to the Pure Land.
We rely upon the great assembly to recite the name of the Pure Dharma Body (*śubha-dharmakāya*) [and so forth]. With each utterance, strike the *kangling* once. Recite the Great [Name].
Recite the Compassionate Mantra once. Then, perform the dedication, saying:
"By the merit of the foregoing recitation and chanting of the sutra, I dedicate it for the sake of the enlightened spirit of the late Elder [Name], to adorn his place of retribution."

I humbly pray that their spirits may transcend to the pure realm and their karmic burdens be shed from the toils of the mundane world. May they bloom as flowers of the highest grade and receive from the Buddha the prediction of their final birth.
Once again, I trouble the venerable assembly to turn their thoughts toward the ten directions and the three periods of time... (and so forth).
Again, having recited the *Śūraṅgama-mantra* once, he performs the ritual circuit and makes the dedication, saying:
"I offer the merit of this scripture recitation for the sake of the enlightened spirit of the newly deceased Elder [Name], to adorn his place of retribution.
Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time... (and so forth).

When the local villagers have completed the offerings at the shrine, the assembly enters their seats to drink soup and recite scriptures such as the *Vajracchedikā* and the *Amitābha Sūtra*, performing the rite of escorting the spirit.
This continues until approximately the end of the second watch, when the merit is dedicated and the assembly disperses. On this day, there may or may not be refreshments;
it is not restricted by whether the deceased had them or not.

The next day, after the morning gruel has been consumed, the public authorities shall assign porters and ropes to complete the preparation of the shrine. Then, the liturgical recitation for raising the shrine shall be performed as follows:
"In order to lift this sacred shrine for the grand rite of cremation, we rely upon the great assembly to chant the vast [mantras] of all the sages."
[Insert Name]. To rectify transgressions against the tablets and to further the path of awakening, we contemplate the pure Dharmakāya (etc.). Thereupon, the rite for raising the coffin was requested.
As the coffin was lifted out of the gate, the assembly each held a willow branch and a piece of firewood, silently reciting sutras and mantras.
He was escorted to the cremation altar. After the abbot had completed the funeral rites and the lighting of the fire, the Rector (Vina) led the ten recitations for the cremation, saying:
"On this day, there is the newly passed away Elder [Name]. Having followed conditions to pass peacefully into stillness, we now perform the cremation according to the Dharma.
We burn the body that practiced the Way for a hundred years, so as to enter the realm of Nirvana on the Single Path. We rely upon..."

The Honored Assembly assists in the rebirth [of the deceased]. Homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One (Recite these ten invocations;
from the four characters "Amitābha Buddha" onwards, the entire assembly shall chant in unison for ten invocations). Thus far, we have extolled the holy name to assist the enlightened spirit.
We pray only that the mirror of wisdom may radiate its brilliance and the true wind may scatter its splendor, so that within the Garden of Bodhi, [the lotus] shall bloom.
Lay out the flowers of the stages of awakening; within the ocean of the *dharmatā*, wash away the defilements of the dusty mind. Pour three libations of tea and burn a single incense burner.
As you escort [the deceased] upon their journey through the clouds, I pay homage to the assembly of sages. Then, recite the Great Compassion Mantra once.
Upon completion, perform the dedication as follows:
The merit from the foregoing recitation and chanting of the sutras is respectfully dedicated to the enlightened spirit of the newly deceased Elder [Name].
At the time of the cremation, may his retribution-ground be adorned; throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time... [and so forth]. Furthermore, the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī is recited.

On that day, the public community prepared a single hall of offerings for the deceased monk. Once the meal was finished, they took out the deceased’s luggage and, before the assembly, verified the seals and opened the packages to lay them out.
The *vinaya-dhara* (chant leader) and the assembly donned their *kāṣāya* robes, struck the *ghaṇṭā* once, and recited as follows:

As drifting clouds disperse, shadows do not remain; as the wick of a dying candle is exhausted, its light naturally extinguishes. Now, this ritual of the auction chant is employed to manifest impermanence.
We look up to rely upon the Great Assembly to recite for the Pure Dharma-body (and so forth).
Upon reaching the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, strike the chime once and say: "I announce to the assembly:

The method for chanting the distribution of robes is used to represent the established rule. Whether new or old, long or short, you should take care of them yourselves. The money must be full-value; do not attempt to substitute it with counterfeit or inferior currency.
Once the sound of the chime has ceased, no regrets shall be permitted. This is respectfully announced."

The officiant takes up the first document inscribed with the character for "Heaven" (天) and places it before the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master). The *vinaya-dhara* first holds up the official document and says:
"One official document accompanying the deceased monk; it shall be torn in the presence of the assembly and submitted to the authorities. He then proceeds to take up the robes one by one and says:
One lot, marked with the character "Tian" (Heaven), consists of one yellow silk *kāṣāya*, mostly new with little old material. One bid equals five hundred copper coins.
Each item is raised in succession. When the auction has concluded, the *qiǎng* is struck once more, and the dedication is recited as follows:
The merit from the foregoing recitation and the chanting of the *kathina* robe is dedicated to the enlightened spirit of the newly deceased Elder [Name],
to adorn his realm of retribution throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, and so forth.
When the chanting for the distribution of robes is finished, the *vinaya-dhara* (weina) shall calculate the estimated costs and record them in a formal ledger (*ban-zhang*).
The public and local people shall go to the altar of the deceased to collect the bones and return with them. They shall further make offerings of incense, flowers, lamps, and candles.
As before, the assembly shall recite scriptures three times daily. On the third day, the bones are escorted away; they may be cremated, scattered into water, or [otherwise disposed of].

Entering the assembly of stupas is likewise a communal rite performed by the great assembly. It includes the ritual for raising the skeletal remains and the ritual for enshrining them within the stupa.

however, having unexpectedly encountered this illness, I fear that my life may not endure. Therefore, I request that the public authorities inventory my personal belongings according to established custom and provide for the transport of my effects to settle my final affairs.
I humbly rely on your favor.

The establishment of monastic registers (*banzhang*) in various regions follows specific regulations; however, the current practice for hermitages (*an*) is not uniform.

One should adopt or reject practices according to what is appropriate and convenient. Although the paths of existence and non-existence differ, their underlying principles of cause and effect (*hetu-phala*) remain the same.

As for the practice of withdrawing one portion from within the wooden screen enclosure, this is an ancient precedent followed in various regions. Since dwelling in a hermitage prioritizes the cultivation of karmic connections, it seems unnecessary to discuss it further.

Ninth, regarding the dedication of merit for the deceased: one should simply enter the shrine room to perform recitations overnight; these three rounds of recitation on the mountain peak are the public ritual.

When dedicating the merit for the *dhātu* (relics), one should address the deceased by their two-character name. For all other occasions, whether public or private, one should simply address them by their second character when dedicating the merit.
When collecting the bones to return for offerings and chanting sutras for dedication, one should simply say "parinirvāṇa" and not "newly parinirvāṇa. Or, in various cases...

When the Venerable Master Fang passed away at the hermitage, and subsequently when Aban [Zhaojue] passed away while serving as abbot, their name tablets were inscribed only with their dharma names, not their two-character secular names;
only the lower character was written, such as "Gong" or "Chan Master.
If a deceased monk has no robes or bowls available for a funeral chant, the hermitage gate should provide the necessary resources to assist in the funeral rites.
If a deceased monk has left his robes and bowl deposited elsewhere and has never issued a written instruction to entrust them to the gatekeeper of the hermitage,
one must not seek to claim them based on hearsay, thereby causing unnecessary trouble.
The Way is the Buddha-work atop the mountain;
on this day, there is indeed a new occurrence. Thus, as the attendant layman [so-and-so] has reached his end according to conditions, we have performed the cremation in accordance with the Dharma.
We burn the body of a hundred years of ascetic practice and enter the realm adorned by the One Path. We look up in reliance upon the Honored One...
The multitude assists a single spirit. *Namo* to Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One.
(Recite ten times.
The above has been the invocation of the Buddha’s name to assist in rebirth. I only pray that the grass will be cleared from the steps and flowers will bloom at the pestle’s tip.
I select that within the Sangha Hall, the invisible *uṣṇīṣa* remains eternally perfect; in the garden of the ancient Buddhas, this impure, defiled body is forever severed.
As the tea is offered in three libations and the incense burned in a single burner, I bid farewell as he journeys upon the clouds. I pay homage to the assembly of sages.
This public property, established as an illusory dwelling, is to be handed over in perpetuity and is not permitted to be lent out.
Text for Opening the Gate of Ambrosia and Universally Bestowing the Dharma-Food:
Recite the Great Compassion Mantra three times and sprinkle pure water.

One must realize that the divine mind is unmoving and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is all-pervasive; since there is no cause for arising or ceasing, how could there be any trace of ascending or sinking?
When the Unsurpassed Dharma King sat upon the precious lotus flower and attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment, what single dharma did he ever add?

All wriggling and breathing sentient beings enter into lands as minute as motes of dust, undergoing transformation through birth and death; yet how could there be the slightest damage to even a single mote?
Thus, the Dragon Girl realized the fruit of enlightenment in the instant she offered her pearl, and Prabhūtaratna attained Buddhahood in the moment he raised his blade.
What distinction can there be between male and female? How could good and evil ever intervene? When they are deluded, even the jeweled nets are all [the same].
The Cakravāḍa mountains, upon reaching enlightenment, become entirely golden ground together with the Sword-Blade Mountains;
thus it is said in the teachings: "Birth is non-birth, for the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is serene; non-birth is birth, for the fruits of karma are majestic.

This is what is meant by saying that phenomena have no fixed characteristics and undergo transformation according to one's thoughts. Now, this great Dharma assembly is inaugurated and wondrous offerings are presented before us. However, as for the five parts...

With this true incense, we invite the Most Holy Ones of the ten directions. Scattering the nectar from a single vessel, we aid the sentient beings of the six realms who share the same spiritual essence.
We proclaim the secret words to bestow empowerment and employ a sincere heart to rescue and deliver them. Desiring to clarify the ultimate principle, I set forth these words.

May the Buddha-work be perfected, and may all together return to the True Limit. (Holding the hand-incense burner) The fragrance of precepts, the fragrance of concentration, the fragrance of wisdom, and the fragrance of liberation...
With incense and the knowledge and vision of liberation, and with clouds of radiant light pervading the entire Dharma-realm,

I single-mindedly entreat all the Buddhas, the assembly of Dharma, and the assembly of Sangha who eternally abide throughout the lands as numerous as atoms within the entirety of space and the Dharma-realm, across the past, present, and future. With a single mind, I entreat you.

Attending upon the Triple Gem and protecting the One Vehicle, within the ranks of the Vaipulya assembly of Radiant Light—manifesting outward majesty while inwardly concealing compassion and forbearance—are the devas, bodhisattvas, eighty thousand vajras, and ten thousand devaputras.

Having accumulated the causes for Bodhi, they have received the Tathāgata’s prediction; wherever they may be, they adorn and purify the Dharma assemblies, leading the multitudes of nāgas and their boundless retinues.
Do not forget your original vow; descend upon this site of practice. We pray that you universally permeate all beings and realize eternal bliss.

May it be so for all humans and devas throughout the dharma-realm. We reverently address the Great Compassionate Father, the Unsurpassed Dharma King: extend your unconditioned, supreme compassion and behold the humble sincerity of sentient beings.
Homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions. Homage to the Dharma of the ten directions. Homage to the Sangha of the ten directions.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Kindness and Great Compassion (three times).

I take refuge in Śākyamuni, the Great Compassionate Father, The supreme gateway of the Jewel Seal Dhāraṇī, To Avalokiteśvara, who received and transmitted the divine mantras, And to Ānanda and the assembly of holy ones who initiated this teaching.
Now, relying upon the sūtra, I recite these secret words To transform these offerings of food and nourish all living beings.
I pray that you grant your majestic light to look upon others, So that the merit of receiving these gifts may be fully realized for all.
Namo sarvatathāgate vairocani oṃ sambhara sambhara hūṃ (seven times). By the empowerment of this divine mantra, may the food and drink be purified;
may it be universally bestowed upon all the spirits and deities as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, so that they may all be fully satisfied and abandon their stinginess.

The mind is immediately liberated from the darkness of the netherworld and reborn in the good realms. Taking refuge in the Triple Gem and generating the bodhicitta, one shall ultimately attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
With boundless merit extending to the end of the future, may all sentient beings partake equally in the Dharma-food.
Namo Śrī Vajra Tathāgatāya. Tadyathā. Oṃ Śrū Śrū.
RU PO RA SU LU PO RA SU LU SVA HĀ (recite seventeen times).
Homage to the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna; homage to the Tathāgata Suvarṇavarṇa; homage to the Tathāgata Vipulaśarīra;
homage to the Tathāgata Abhayaviraja; homage to the Tathāgata Amṛtendrarāja.
Oṃ gagaṇasvabhāva vajra hūṃ (Recite three times; strike the *cī* once upon taking one’s seat). O children of the Buddhas:
if anyone wishes to thoroughly understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate the nature of the dharma-dhātu;
all is but the creation of the mind. This single verse is from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. In the past, when someone recited it before a minister of the underworld, he saw the earth...
The characteristics of the hells are all completely shattered; the world tradition calls this the "Verses for Shattering Hell. This is merely a brief statement.
To speak of it extensively, these verses not only shatter hell, but are capable of shattering all ten dharma realms. Why is this?
Originally, when there were no Buddhas throughout the three periods of time, what nature did the dharma realm possess? It was established entirely upon this one mind. To fully realize this—
The mind is signless and without substance; it is neither form nor emptiness. It is non-existent yet existent, non-nonexistent yet nonexistent.
Because it is not existent, the ten dharma realms are subsumed within a single hair-tip; because it is not nonexistent, the Buddhas of the three periods of time arise everywhere.
Thus it is said: "The lush green bamboo is entirely True Suchness (Tathatā); the dense yellow flowers are all Prajñā. If this is indeed so, then...
The four modes of birth and the six realms of existence are entirely one’s own mind. The eight difficulties and the three miserable paths are not obtained from elsewhere.

This is truly because the emotions harbor attachment and views, while one's traces involve superior conditions. By means of this, the five precepts are upheld and the ten wholesome acts are cultivated and advanced.

When karmic retribution and conditions meet, one proceeds from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven up to the Four Formless Heavens; this is called the heavenly realm. The root of the mind is desire and love, and consciousness carries the burden of discernment.
Illumination: Movement does not depart from the Five Constant Virtues; dwelling in the world, one does not forget the hundred practices.

From the three teachings and nine schools to the four classes and myriad people—whether poor or wealthy, noble or humble, good or evil, wise or foolish—they all merely follow the wheel of karma as they transmigrate. This is called the human way.
When desire and hatred are combined with superior views, strife does not cease, and what purpose is served by such stubbornness? Only through merit can there be peace.

Deprived of the blessings of the heavenly kin, they fall into the realm of ghosts; this is called the path of the asuras. Although these three classes possess the faculty of faith, they are entirely encompassed by outflows (*āsrava*).
They temporarily ascend according to their karma and are thus termed the "three good paths. Yet, when craving and views enter the mind, they give rise to the karma of greed.
Seeking falsely and never satisfied, their anxieties hang heavy day and night. Thus, the karma of greed manifests within as thirst and hunger, and without...
Thus they become wind and flame; this is the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). When desire and greed do not cease, they revolve into delusion (*moha*);

as their mental perceptions fluctuate, they rise or sink according to their karma. With scales, shells, and feathers, their forms and appearances number in the thousands—this is called the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*).

When the ten habitual practices are not severed and the six modes of interaction entwine and ensnare them, they encounter swords, pits, volcanic mountains, iron wheels, boiling cauldrons, and scorching pots; they are suspended upside down, cast down from heights, or bound and fettered.
Investigation and examination reveal that the eight cold and eight hot hells, extending to the Avīci Hell, are called the hell realm (*naraka-gati*).

These three categories [of beings], having no virtuous causes and further nourishing greed and other afflictions, endure suffering that cannot be exhausted even if space itself were to end; thus they are called the three evil realms (*durgati*).

The first three [realms] are the virtuous classes, and the latter three are the evil classes; together they are collectively termed the six realms (*ṣadgati*). Thus they circulate in transmigration for aeons as numerous as motes of dust, or perhaps—
There will be no time when one turns the mind back toward the Way. How do we know this? The ancient teachings state: "Because of karma one receives a body, and the body in turn creates karma;
from the mind arise objects, and objects in turn give rise to the mind. Thus we know that karma is created by the body and objects originate from the mind.
Wandering through every place and revolving in every thought-moment, from birth until death, from beginning to end, it is like an elephant sinking in mud.
Like mud in which ants turn in circles, our Buddha, the Great Śramaṇa, gives rise to great compassion within the state of non-seeing.
By means of his wondrous power of non-action, when he burns it, it becomes incense that universally perfumes; when he scatters it, it becomes flowers that spread everywhere.
Yet, when offered as lamps, they illuminate all together; when sprinkled as water, they moisten all equally; when presented as fruit, there is nothing that is not made magnificent;
when bestowed as food, all obtain full satisfaction. Even so, the wealth of all dharmas is obtained in accordance with whatever is sought.
This is called the seven kinds of sublime offerings, which are of one flavor of true compassion, directed toward every Buddha in every thought-moment.

Birth. Although these qualities are fully present within each and every sentient being, because the sons of the Buddhas are deeply entangled in the burdens of karma, they rarely possess the true cause.
It is as if the light of a divine mirror is obscured by accumulated dust, or as if the essence of refined gold is mixed with base ore.
Now, I first repent for the karmic obstructions of all the sons of the Buddhas; thereafter, taking refuge in the Triple Gem, I shall confer upon them the five [precepts].
They uphold the pure precepts and fulfill the four great vows, giving rise to the Bodhicitta for the Way. Such Buddha-works are perfectly accomplished in their respective places;
each manifests an Udumbara flower in the field of birth and nirvana. Who here is ordinary and who there is holy?
They ripen the fruit of Bodhi upon the ground of past rising and sinking. Now there is no awakening, and in the past there was no delusion. It is not merely a dream of the six realms.

My soul is dissolved with anticipation. I shall now behold the provisional names of the Four Truths. Relying now upon the holy teachings, I shall, on behalf of all the sons of the Buddha, repent for their transgressions and evils.
I entreat the entire assembly to join me in chanting in unison.
All evil karma created in the past, arising from beginningless greed, anger, and ignorance,
produced by body, speech, and mind— I now repent of it all (recite three times).
I now possess a mantra for extinguishing karmic obstacles.
All you sons of the Buddha, listen with a sincere and attentive mind. Oṃ sarvapāpaviśuddhanāthavajrāya svāhā.
"O sons of the Buddha, having purified yourselves through repentance, you should now take refuge in the Triple Gem. Now, as for the Triple Gem, there are many different aspects;
here I shall explain them only briefly. The King of Golden Features, seated upon a precious lotus flower, is called the Buddha-Gem.
The lapis lazuli caskets and palm-leaf manuscripts filling the Vairocana-treasury are called the Dharma-Gem. Those with square robes and shaven heads, unstained by worldly dust, are called the..."

The Sangha Jewel. This refers to the Three Jewels as maintained through formal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). One must know that within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), the Three Jewels are fully present.
The fundamental essence (*dharmatā*) of a single thought-moment, which is free from all names and characteristics, is called the Buddha Jewel.

The manifestation of this essence through its function, wherein the *dharmadhātu* is manifest in its full majesty, is named the Dharma Jewel. The mutual penetration of essence and function, where principle and phenomenon are non-dual, is designated as the Sangha Jewel. Now, first...
First take refuge in and dwell upon the Three Jewels as the Sustainers; thereafter, suddenly clarify the Three Jewels of One Substance within yourself.
This is what is meant by "proceeding from the shallow to the profound. I shall now speak on your behalf; let us all join our voices in chanting together.

I take refuge in the Buddha, the Unsurpassed Honored One. I take refuge in the Dharma, the Honored One who is free from desire. I take refuge in the Saṅgha, the Honored One among the multitude. By taking refuge in the Buddha, one does not fall into hell.
By taking refuge in the Dharma, one does not fall among the hungry ghosts. By taking refuge in the Saṅgha, one does not fall among the animals.
Having completed my refuge in the Buddha, having completed my refuge in the Dharma, and having completed my refuge in the Saṅgha—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—is my [refuge].
"Great Master, I now take refuge in you; I vow never to take refuge in demons, heretics, or external paths. I pray only that the Triple Gem will look upon me with compassion.
(Recite this three times.)
Now there is a mantra for taking refuge in the Triple Gem; listen with a sincere and attentive mind. Oṃ bhuḥ khaṃ.
You, sons of the Buddha, since you have thus proclaimed the Buddha as your teacher, you shall receive the pure precepts of the Tathāgata.
I shall now, in accordance with the teachings, proclaim for you the characteristics of the five-limbed pure precepts.
Now, refraining from taking life is the characteristic of the five precepts. To examine the root of killing, it has anger as its basis. When the karma of anger is intense, acts of slaughter increase.

Lives are taken and given in mutual debt, revolving in a cycle of retribution. Whether one kills oneself or incites others to kill, if the intent to kill is not eliminated, the cycle of saṃsāra will not cease.
Therefore, for as long as one lives, one must refrain from taking life.

Abstaining from stealing is the characteristic of the fifth precept. Originally, stealing has the karma of greed as its root. As long as the karma of greed is not exhausted, the mind of theft will not cease.
When the hidden mechanisms are activated, terror arises abruptly; through the cycles of past and future, there is mutual retribution.

To steal for oneself and to incite others to steal, with the mind of theft never ceasing, one cannot distance oneself from the defilements. Therefore, for as long as life lasts, one must refrain from stealing.

Refraining from sexual misconduct is the characteristic of the fifth precept. Originally, the root of the karma of lust lies in the poison of delusion; the waters of craving drown the mind and transform it.

It is the fire of desire. There is no receiving of form or inheriting of life that does not proceed from this. From committing sexual misconduct oneself to teaching others to commit it—if the lustful mind is not eliminated, how can the defilements ever come to an end?
Therefore, for as long as one lives, one must refrain from sexual desire.

Abstaining from false speech is the characteristic of the fifth precept. To examine the nature of false speech, it is as previously described regarding the karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct:

they mutually conceal one another so that one does not realize them. Once these empty falsehoods are established, the karma of delusion is formed; this, in turn, provides the support for greed and other afflictions.

Deceiving oneself and teaching others to deceive, one is bound within the cycle of birth and death with no prospect of escape. Therefore, for the remainder of one’s life, one must refrain from false speech.
Abstaining from intoxicants is the characteristic of the fifth precept. To examine its origins: drinking alcohol can cloud right mindfulness and disturb the right mind;

when one is clouded and distracted, there is no time when deviant errors do not arise. The aforementioned four precepts are produced because of this. It is better to drink poisonous medicine than to crave the taste of alcohol.

Whether drinking it oneself or teaching others to drink, the faults of alcohol are fully described and could not be exhausted even throughout accumulated kalpas. Therefore, for as long as one lives, one should [abstain from it].
Do not drink alcohol.
The teachings of the Name (Confucianism) state that if one does not uphold the five precepts, the path to the realms of humans and devas is cut off.

Furthermore, beyond the five precepts, there are the ten inexhaustible precepts, the forty-eight minor defilement precepts, the two hundred and fifty major precepts, and the three clusters of pure precepts.
The purity of the precepts is inexhaustible. It is like a person entering the ocean, who goes deeper and deeper as they advance;
if you simply maintain faith without regressing, then all the precepts will naturally enter your heart.
"O sons of the Buddha, having now fully received the pure precepts of the Tathāgata, you should give rise to the bodhicitta and fulfill the four great vows.
For the four great vows are the function of the bodhicitta, while the bodhicitta is the essence of the four great vows.
Among the Buddhas of the three periods and the boundless bodhisattvas, there has never been one who did not possess these."
For those who have made the vow to attain the path of Bodhi and whose resolve does not regress, I shall lead the chant; you should respond in harmony with me:
"I vow to deliver boundless sentient beings; I vow to sever inexhaustible afflictions; I vow to study immeasurable Dharma gates;
I vow to realize the unattainable Buddha-way. (Thus chant three times.)
O Sons of the Buddha, since your vows are so vast, if you do not give rise to the bodhicitta, they will inevitably become empty formalities. Now, as for this bodhicitta:
all Buddhas of the past have already given rise to it; all Buddhas of the present are now giving rise to it; and all Buddhas of the future shall give rise to it.
Indeed, the bodhicitta is the womb from which Buddhas and patriarchs are conceived; it is the ladder by which they ascend; it is the vessel by which they ferry others across;

and it is the gateway through which they emerge. You, sons of the Buddha, if you do not give rise to the bodhicitta, there is no way to escape the river of craving, no way to break free from the bonds of suffering, no way to purify the feverish afflictions, and no way to realize the Buddha-vehicle. You should know this.

The essence of bodhicitta is free from the characteristics of seeing and hearing; it is free from the characteristics of verbal expression; it is free from the characteristics of conceptual thought; indeed, it is free from all characteristics whatsoever.

O sons of the Buddha, if you wish to realize this bodhicitta, you should contemplate that the four great elements are without self, the three realms are without phenomena, the eight consciousnesses have no master, and the six destinies have no person. By observing in this way, delusion is itself delusion and awakening is itself awakening.
One also awakens to this for oneself. Pleasure is one's own pleasure; suffering is likewise one's own suffering. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"To know that all phenomena are the very nature of mind is to achieve the body of wisdom, which does not depend on awakening through another. Such a teaching reveals the truth directly before one's eyes.

It values nothing more than the individual’s own total capacity to receive and bear this realization. Therefore it is said: "The myriad phenomena are the radiance of the mind; all conditions are the clarity of the nature."
Fundamentally, there is no person who is deluded or awakened; it simply requires realization this very day (thereupon snapping his fingers three times).
O sons of the Buddha! It comes directly down: the light of bodhicitta pervades the faculty of the eye, and the sound of bodhicitta fully returns to the locus of the ear.
Thus, one is not deluded by pleasures within the three happy realms, nor is one [deluded] within the three evil realms.
That which is grasped as suffering is but mind; the Buddha is likewise but mind. Sentient beings are likewise but the Buddha. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
O sons of the Buddha, from this day forward, take the bodhicitta as your dwelling and abide therein with freedom;
take the bodhicitta as your grove and wander therein without hindrance; take the bodhicitta as your bed and seat.

Dwelling in leisure and ease, take the bodhicitta as your teacher and achieve samādhi; enter the nature-ocean of Vairocana in every speck of dust, and meet the gateways of spiritual friends everywhere.
This may be called reaching the City of Enlightenment without moving a single step, and returning entirely to the Treasure Abode without being separated by a single particle of dust.
Now I have a mantra for generating the bodhicitta; listen with a sincere and attentive mind.
Oṃ maitrīcitta-mudrapanaya me. Having recited one scroll of the Heart Sūtra, the dedication is made as follows:
"You hosts of spirits and deities, I now bestow this offering upon you. May this food pervade the ten directions and be shared by all spirits and deities."
"May these merits be universally extended to all. May we and all sentient beings together attain the Buddha-way.
If this is during a *yulanpen* fast, one may alter the subsequent prose after the first strike of the *chishi* (wooden ruler) upon taking one's seat;
the verses for repentance shall likewise conclude with the same wording as before.
O Sons of the Buddha: The Sanskrit term for *Ullambana* means "vessel for relieving the inverted suspension.

As for those who are "invertedly suspended," their forms are bound to the summit of a thousand-fathom precipice, on the verge of falling into the bottomless abyss; the word "suffering" alone cannot serve as a metaphor for it.
Originally, within the equal and true Dharma-realm, there is neither Buddha nor sentient being; how, then, could there be any talk of inverted suspension?
Indeed, this arises fundamentally from the initial lack of awakening, whereby a deluded mind suddenly stirs. Externally, it manifests the distinctions between the ten realms of defilement and purity;

internally, it harbors the differences between the eight consciousnesses regarding enlightenment and delusion. Consequently, one binds the substance of ignorance with the ropes of false views, hanging head-downward atop the thousand-fathom precipice of the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses.
Looking down, one gazes upon the bottomless depths of the cycle of birth and death. All phenomena...
The winds of the realms shake and toss them from moment to moment without ceasing; thus, the sages and worthies regard them as objects of pity.

For this reason, compassion arises though not intended to arise, and sorrow arrives though not intended to arrive. How much more so for Cing-t'i (Candika), who has committed grave offenses and is difficult to rescue, and for Maudgalyāyana, whose feelings are profound and who desires to follow after him.
This opens up the fundamental intention of the Tathāgata and fulfills the great vow of the Bodhisattva.

The teachings have reached us through this transmission for over two thousand years. Since there are dwelling places of the Buddhas, how could one not emulate these excellent regulations and follow these superior tracks?
The above secret mantras have been empowered to bestow nectar universally; imagine that all you sons of the Buddha are now fully satiated.
Yet, if you do not penetrate the fundamental source of the Way and clearly perceive the fountainhead of the Dharma, you will not only remain hungry and in a state of inverted suspension, but now—

Though they may be satiated, they have never ceased to be in a state of inverted suspension. Not only regarding satiety, but even considering that among the six realms of existence, the heavens are supreme:
the fundamental cause for rebirth there lies in abandoning all evils, delighting in the cultivation of various virtues, and aspiring for the fruits of merit to transcend this class of beings.
Yet, as long as the true mind remains unawakened, one has already entered a state of inverted suspension; how much more so when the food and drink of the seven treasures follow every whim of desire?
Thus, transformations arise. Garments and crowns made of a hundred jewels are displayed according to the inclinations of the heart; the celestial hosts take pleasure in observing these adornments.
Yet only the Buddha’s knowledge and vision recognize this as a true state of inverted suspension—how much more so when one encounters the five signs of decline?

Now, within the seas of the world, human beings are densely populated; they occupy the rank immediately below that of the heavens. Their attachments and defilements do not cease, even as they intermingle with various virtuous deeds.

Coming to this human realm, those whose bodies occupy the highest rank are called noble; those whose households store much gold are called wealthy; those who have extensively studied the elegant language are called wise;
and those who have fully mastered the *Spring and Autumn Annals* are called long-lived. Yet, even they may not suddenly clarify the ultimate principle or attain a vast awakening to the True Constant;

when their single lifetime abruptly ends, how can they find peace or release from their inverted suspension? This is all the more so for the crippled, the widowed, the orphaned, and the destitute who remain in a state of lingering suffering. Relying upon...
In the state of perfect emptiness, birth and death are without reliance; yet how could this depend upon the exhaustion of karmic retribution?

The traces of such suspended existence are present at all times. Asuras belong to the category next to that of humans. Because they seek the fruits of merit with partiality and cling solely to a sense of superiority, they accumulate desire and greed, causing these beings to sink [into lower realms].
There are those without merit who fall into the realm of hungry ghosts, and those with merit who belong to the class of devas. By means of...
Those who do not forget their anger and strife hang themselves upside down, suffering in self-inflicted torment. When will their karma reach its limit? When will the end of their retribution come?
They will be cast away and lost forever, falling into the bottomless abyss. This is the "upside-down hanging" of the three lower realms of existence.

It is for these beings that the King of Great Compassionate Vows feels deep pity and profound sorrow. If the "upside-down hanging" of the three lower realms is such as this, how much more so for those in the hells and the realm of hungry ghosts!
How can one fully describe the suffering of the three kinds of animal rebirths and the inverted hanging of the evil realms? All these are caused by greed, hatred, and delusion;
they take killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct as their conditions; and the desire realm, form realm, and formless realm constitute their retributive fruits.
Within the hells, they become iron wheels when mounted upon, sword-blades when trodden upon, flying objects when moved, and [solid ground] when at rest.
They are imprisoned and bound; thus, the sufferings of the eight cold and eight hot hells, up to the Avīci hell and the agony of being hung upside down, reach their ultimate limit here.
Once the retribution of the hells has been exhausted, they disperse their forms and enter the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). Their physical bodies are already hollow and lack majestic radiance.
They dwell perpetually in foul crevices and always travel upon dark paths. When thirsty, they find water that instantly turns into molten copper;

when hungry, they encounter food that suddenly transforms into blazing flames. They suffer from hunger and starvation for hundreds of kalpas, and remain submerged in profound darkness for twelve hours at a time.

He spoke in detail of their bitter sufferings, which do not end with being hung upside down. When their karma in the realm of ghosts is exhausted, they scatter into the animal realm to repay their past debts;
they fly through the air, leap across waters, nest in trees, or dwell upon mountains, where the strong swallow the weak and the large devour the small.

The grief of being torn apart by [saws and axes] is unceasing; the suffering of being devoured and consumed is endless. The species with feathers and fur are already numerous, and those of the scaly and shelled families are even more abundant.
As their evil karma grows ever more intense, their forms become increasingly distorted; the crawling, wriggling, flying, and fluttering creatures are too many to be enumerated.

Their liver and intestines are scorched in cauldrons; their bones and blood are crushed upon butcher’s blocks. This so-called "hanging upside down" is perhaps insufficient to fully illustrate the suffering of the animal realm.
As for the suffering of those in the three evil paths who hang upside down, were one to describe it in detail, it would not be exhausted even throughout an entire kalpa.

To summarize: even the ascent to the three good paths is like hanging upside down if one has not yet clarified the fundamental nature of the Way. Thus, even in the three [good paths], there is still the state of being inverted.
Sunk in the evil realms, they do not awaken to the causes of suffering; their inverted suspension continues without end. You should know this:

the Buddhas are those who have already untied the inverted suspension of sentient beings, while sentient beings are those Buddhas who have not yet untied their own inverted suspension. Once the inverted suspension is untied, the realm of sentient beings is exhausted and the essence of the Buddhas is revealed as empty.
They turn the three virtuous paths back toward the Heaven of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-dhātu*), and the clouds of delusion naturally disperse.

[This] volume [describes how one] melts away all evil destinies and enters the ocean of true samādhi. The waves of karma subside and sink; it is like a long-traveling guest arriving home, or a poor man encountering a treasure.
The teachings of the Name say: when sentient beings are deluded, they point to gold and call it copper;

yet when they attain awakening, they clearly understand the essence of the gold. Not understanding that they were hanging upside down, they falsely claimed there were six realms of existence. Now that the inverted suspension has been resolved, this is [the state of liberation].

With single-minded devotion, the Buddhas, within their state of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*), take pity upon the sons of the Buddha who have deeply cast themselves into the net of karma and long remained stranded on the dark path.
Within this very mind, they burn it as incense, scatter it as flowers, offer it as lamps, bestow it as food, present it as fruit, and scoop it up as ointment;
thus, through inexhaustible Dharma-wealth, they fulfill the seven types of offerings.
Make offerings. These are specially prepared as adornments for all the sons of the Buddhas.
Once these adornments are complete, if one does not lay them out and repent of past and present actions of body, speech, and mind, then the state of being head-downward suspended cannot be resolved.

Having already repented, if one does not take refuge in the Triple Gem and acknowledge the Buddha as Teacher, then the state of being head-downward suspended cannot be resolved. Having already taken refuge in the Triple Gem, if...
If one does not fully receive the Tathāgata’s truly pure precepts, then the state of being inverted and suspended cannot be resolved.
Once the precepts have been received, if one does not establish the four great vows and resolve the mind for Bodhi, then the state of being inverted and suspended cannot be resolved.
One should know that everything from self-repentance up to the resolution for Bodhi constitutes the skillful means for resolving this state of being inverted and suspended. I now, relying upon...
Relying upon the sacred teachings, we first repent for the ten unwholesome karmas committed by body, speech, and mind throughout our lives as children of the Buddhas.

We look up to the great assembly to each apply a sincere heart and join me in recitation. You, sons of the Buddhas, should conceive the thought that this encounter is difficult to find and maintain a spirit of longing;
listen attentively, listen attentively! All the evil karma created in the past arises from beginningless greed and anger.
Delusion arises from body, speech, and mind. I now repent of it all (recite this three times).
I now possess a mantra for extinguishing karmic obstacles; all you sons of the Buddha, listen with a sincere heart and with careful attention.
Oṃ sarvabāpaviṣphoṭanahana vajrāyāvaha.
I, the śramaṇa [Name], of the Huanzhu Chan Hermitage on Mount Bian, in the City North of Huzhou Prefecture, under the Road of Zhexi, Great Yuan State—
hereby respectfully disclose my sincere heart to Your Majesty, the Great Creator,
and pray that You will deign to grant [Your favor].

To my parents of past lives and my parents and teachers of this present life, to my benefactors, to those who have been both benefactors and enemies,

flowers, lamps, candles, tea, fruit, and exquisite delicacies to offer according to the Dharma.
The Sangha of the eternally abiding Triple Gem, the Dharma-realm, and the noble sages, including the monastic assembly,
don the armor of the Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra and the Mahāyāna Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra.
The Mahāvaipulya Sūtra on Perfect Enlightenment: The Definitive Meaning;
The Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra of the Great Buddha-Crown, the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, and the Ten Thousand Practices of All Bodhisattvas.

and the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama Divine Mantra of the Myriad Practices. [These are] extolled.
The Holy Name of the Mahābuddhamātṛ.
I offer this single vessel of pure, impartial, and vast nectar-like Dharma-food as a fulfillment and distribution.
May the aforementioned accumulated merits be dedicated with a single mind to all within the Dharmadhātu.
The hosts of the deva realm, the human realm, the asura realm, the hell realm, the preta realm, and the animal realm— may you all,
by the power of the Buddha, come to this Dharma assembly. With single-minded devotion, we offer this for [the sake of]...
To all past and present masters who have provided guidance, encouragement, and inspiration through skillful means, who have acted as preceptors and teachers,

and who have performed the rites of tonsure and ordination for all disciples, friends, and kinsmen; and to those who, discerning this sincerity, have likewise proceeded to this Dharma assembly— to them, and with single-minded devotion,

we dedicate these merits for the sake of our co-resident monks and nuns, each of our own biological parents, our ancestors of seven generations, and all those who have assumed form throughout past kalpas.
For all parents from whom we have received our lives throughout accumulated births, may they,
through the power of the Buddha, equally partake of the nectar of immortality. With single-minded devotion,
we offer this for the sake of all great donors and external protectors who provided the four requisites during past kalpas and within the present world.

May the Dharma-teachers, kings, lords, ministers, governors, officials of the prefectures, counties, and towns, civil and military functionaries, elders, titled ladies, lay devotees, spiritual friends,
and all disciples who inquire after the Way and seek instruction, likewise ride upon this [merit] to descend together to this Dharma assembly; may you all focus your minds with single-mindedness.
On behalf of all solitary spirits and lingering souls— whether from the nine provinces and twelve regions, from distant lands or nearby places,
male or female, old or young, dwelling in the air or on water, whether scaly, feathered, or otherwise sentient or insentient beings— [I offer this].
Together with those of like kind, we ride upon the power of the Buddha to attend this Dharma assembly.

With single-minded devotion, we dedicate [this merit] for the sake of all sentient beings—past, present, and future—within all lands as numerous as atoms throughout the entirety of empty space and the Dharma-realm:

those who are submerged in the ocean of suffering, or drowning in the river of craving; those dwelling in the forest of heterodoxy, or lurking in dark chambers; or those residing on the shores of the waters.
Some fall from the tops of cliffs; some dwell in perilous places or nest in filthy crevices; some reside in hollows or remain trapped in the dark underworld.
Even in such various unwholesome states and amidst masses of evil, they are entangled by their shared karma, lacking any thought of repentance or awakening.

Although one may rely on the successive vehicles, a true salvation that transcends the realms has yet to be attained. I pray that by means of the universal compassion of this very night, the heavy defilements accumulated over many lifetimes may be simultaneously purified.

I humbly submit that within the minds of all Buddhas dwell sentient beings, who have bound themselves with the profound karmic actions of the ocean of the Dharma-realm; and within the minds of sentient beings...

The Buddhas within [the realm] give rise to the compassion of the *Ullambana* for universal salvation. Through a single thought of awakening or delusion, the suffering and joy of the three periods of time are formed.
The mountain of blades and the pit of swords all become the field of Equal and Right Enlightenment; the jeweled ground and the jade steps are but the domain where one drifts and falls into saṃsāra.
How can the transformations of one's own karma be fathomed? The manifestations of the mind-dharma are inexhaustible. What is... [the limit]?

As the ancient masters have said: "The falling away is not some other thing; whether horizontal or vertical, it is not defilement. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all fully reveal the body of the Dharma King.
If one realizes this meaning, one knows where to return in that very place. One merges with the self-mind of all Buddha-sons and enters the true limit of Great Nirvana.
In every place there is no suffering to be weary of; in every place there is no joy to be delighted in.

When the grasping and rejecting of every particle of dust are forgotten, and the likes and dislikes of every thought-moment are exhausted, what enemy remains to be reconciled and what relative remains to rely upon?
Afflictions are themselves bodhi; one suddenly realizes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom. Ignorance is itself liberation; it entirely encompasses the body of supreme merit.
Within the shadow of purple sandalwood, as one bows, turns, and moves, the flowing water is originally the ocean. Amidst the red lotus flowers...
In the interim, through seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, one realizes that the moon’s descent does not depart from the sky. At this very moment, one is satiated with the flavor of nectar;
throughout eternal kalpas, the udumbara flower manifests.
